name: René Descartes, A Discourse on the Method (1637)
description: The argument structure of Descartes' Discourse on the Method, rendered as a worldview. Every statement is written in Descartes' first person and every argument records an inference he draws, or visibly relies on, in the text. All six parts are covered: the review of the sciences (I), the four precepts of the method (II), the provisional morality (III), the metaphysics of the cogito, God and the soul (IV), the physics, the physiology of the heart, and the animal-machine argument (V), and the reasons for and against publishing (VI). Cross-part links are made explicit: the method is applied in the doubt of Part IV, the morality rests on the resolve of Part II, the criterion of clear and distinct perception carries the metaphysics into the physics, and the decisions of Part VI rest on the duty to promote the general good of mankind.

source.title: Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting the Reason, and Seeking Truth in the Sciences
source.author: René Descartes

extraction.method: LLM-assisted close reading, part by part, merged, then adversarially reviewed against the text

meta.note: How to read citations: meta.source lists paragraph keys such as "IV.3" (Part IV, paragraph 3) into the local text, where every paragraph is tagged. A statement's citations are the paragraphs where it is asserted or where an inference Descartes draws relies on it (a reconstructed link adds no citation to its premises, since Descartes does not invoke them there); an argument's are the paragraphs where the inference is drawn, the primary one first. meta.role is an informal label (observation, assumption, definition, rule, maxim, axiom, conclusion) recording how the text presents the statement, not its position in the graph; the format defines no vocabulary. A statement whose note begins 'Implicit' marks a hidden premise the text relies on without stating (its role is usually 'assumption'); an argument whose note begins 'Reconstructed link' records an inference the editor supplied rather than one Descartes draws in the cited paragraph: either a dependency between parts or paragraphs made explicit when the six per-part extractions were merged and reviewed, or a step the text states without reasoning; its justification is the editor's reading, not Descartes' words. Some statements are a contrast case, occasion, illustration or concession that Descartes states alongside an inference; they are kept, with a note saying so, but are not premises. Nothing here is an endorsement: the file records what Descartes argued, not what is true. One cycle is deliberate. The criterion that whatever is clearly and distinctly conceived is true is derived from the cogito (IV.3) and then used to establish God's existence (IV.5), while God's existence and veracity are in turn said to be what makes the criterion certain (IV.7). This is the Cartesian circle; the file represents it honestly as a strongly connected component (clear-and-distinct-is-true, geometry-certain-because-clearly-conceived, god-exists, god-has-all-perfections), which the format allows by design. Both statements also have non-circular support, so nothing is left ungrounded by it.

statements.text: Everyone thinks himself so well supplied with good sense that even those hardest to satisfy in everything else do not usually wish for more of it.
It is not likely that everyone is mistaken about this.

meta.note: Stated in passing; it is what turns the universal conviction about good sense into evidence of its equal distribution.

statements.text: Good sense, or reason, is the power of judging rightly and distinguishing truth from error.
Good sense, the power of judging rightly and distinguishing truth from error, is by nature equal in all men.

meta.note: The opening claim of the Discourse. Part VI.11 relies on it again when Descartes says that readers who use their unprejudiced natural reason will be the best judges of his opinions.

statements.text: The diversity of our opinions does not arise from some having more reason than others, but from conducting our thoughts along different paths and attending to different things.
To have a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is to apply it rightly.
The greatest minds are open to the greatest aberrations, and those who go slowly but keep to the straight road outstrip those who run and leave it.
I have never thought my mind in any respect more perfect than those of the common run of men.
I have often wished that I were equal to some others in promptitude of thought, in clearness and distinctness of imagination, or in fullness and readiness of memory.
Besides promptitude of thought, imagination and memory, I know of no other quality that contributes to the perfection of the mind except reason.

meta.note: Stated in passing; it closes the enumeration.

statements.text: Reason, or good sense, is what alone constitutes us as men and distinguishes us from the brutes.
What alone constitutes us men belongs to our form or nature, not to our accidents.

meta.note: Implicit. Needed to move from reason constituting us men to reason being a form, not an accident.

statements.text: As the philosophers commonly hold, more and less occur only among the accidents, not among the forms or natures of individuals of the same species.

meta.note: A scholastic doctrine Descartes explicitly adopts here to ground the completeness of reason in each individual.

statements.text: My method gives me the means, as I think, of gradually augmenting my knowledge and raising it little by little to the highest point that the mediocrity of my talents and the brief duration of my life will permit.

meta.note: Formed from considerations and maxims Descartes says he fell in with very early in life by singular good fortune (I.3).

statements.text: I have already reaped such fruits from my method that I take the highest satisfaction in the progress I believe I have made in the search for truth.
Looking as a philosopher at the varied pursuits of mankind, I find scarcely one that does not appear vain and useless.
If any occupation of men as men is truly excellent and important, it is the search for truth that I have chosen.
We are very liable to delusion in what concerns ourselves, and the judgments of friends given in our favor are to be suspected.
I may be mistaken about my progress; perhaps what I take for gold and diamonds is only copper and glass.
I should describe the paths I have followed, so that each reader may judge them for himself and the general opinion of them becomes a new aid to my instruction.
Those who set themselves to give precepts must regard themselves as more skilled than those they prescribe to, and are censured if they err in the slightest.
I should not teach the method that everyone ought to follow, but only describe, as a history or, if you will, a tale, how I have tried to conduct my own reason.
Put forth merely as a history, or a tale, with some examples worth imitating and perhaps as many better not followed, this discourse may prove useful to some without being hurtful to any.
I was given to believe that through letters a clear and certain knowledge of all that is useful in life could be acquired, and so I ardently desired instruction.

meta.note: A belief instilled by his teachers; it sets the standard of 'science' against which his education is then found wanting.

statements.text: On finishing the entire course of study, I found myself in so many doubts and errors that I had gained nothing but the discovery of my own ignorance.
I studied at one of the most celebrated schools in Europe, where learned men must be found if they are to be found anywhere.
I was taught all that others learned there, and in addition read all the books that came into my hands on the branches esteemed most curious and rare.
I was not considered inferior to my fellows, some already marked out to succeed our instructors, and our age seemed as fertile in powerful minds as any before it.
I may take the liberty of judging all other men by myself.

meta.note: Descartes says he was 'led to take the liberty'; it is the licence that lets his own case stand for everyone's.

statements.text: There is no science in existence of the kind I had been led to believe in.

The languages of the schools are needed to read the ancients; fable stirs the mind, history elevates it and, read with discretion, helps form judgment, and excellent books converse with the noblest minds.
Eloquence has incomparable force and beauty, and poetry has ravishing graces and delights.
Mathematics contains many refined discoveries that gratify the inquisitive, further all the arts, and lessen the labor of man.
Treatises on morals contain many highly useful precepts and exhortations to virtue.
Theology points out the path to heaven, and I revere it and aspire as much as anyone to reach heaven.
Philosophy affords the means of discoursing with an appearance of truth on all matters, and commands the admiration of the simple.
Jurisprudence, medicine, and the other sciences secure honors and riches for those who cultivate them.
It is useful to give some attention to all studies, even those fullest of superstition and error, to learn their real value and guard against being deceived by them.
I still continued to hold the studies of the schools in esteem.
To hold converse with those of other ages through their writings is almost the same as to travel.
Knowing something of the manners of other nations lets us judge our own more soundly and keeps us from thinking everything contrary to our customs ridiculous and irrational.
Too much time spent traveling makes us strangers to our own country, and those over-curious about the past are generally ignorant of the present.
Fables make us imagine impossible things possible, and even the most faithful histories omit the meanest circumstances, so that what remains does not represent the truth.
Those who regulate their conduct by examples drawn from histories are apt to fall into the extravagances of knights-errant and to entertain projects beyond their powers.
I had already given sufficient time to languages and to reading the ancients, their histories and their fables.

Those in whom reason predominates and who best order their thoughts to make them clear and intelligible persuade best, even speaking only the language of Lower Brittany and wholly ignorant of the rules of rhetoric.
Those whose minds hold the most agreeable fancies and express them with the most embellishment and harmony are the best poets, even without the art of poetry.
Eloquence and poetry are gifts of nature rather than fruits of study.
The reasonings of mathematics are certain and evident, and this above all delighted me in them.

meta.note: Part II builds on this: the mathematicians alone have found demonstrations, so their order of reasoning becomes the model for the method.

statements.text: I did not yet know the true use of mathematics, and thought it contributed only to the advancement of the mechanical arts.
Mathematics offers foundations strong and solid, yet nothing loftier than the mechanical arts has been raised on them, which astonished me.
The ancient moralists laud the virtues far above anything on earth, yet give no adequate criterion of virtue, and often what they so name is only apathy, pride, despair, or parricide.
The moral writings of the ancients are like towering, magnificent palaces with no better foundation than sand and mud.
Nothing solid can be built on foundations that are not themselves certain.

meta.note: Implicit. Never stated as a principle, but relied on in the images of palaces on sand and of superstructures on infirm foundations; it is also the root of the Part II resolve to rebuild from the foundations.

statements.text: The way to heaven is no less open to the most ignorant than to the most learned.

meta.note: Something Descartes was 'given assuredly to understand'; accepted on authority, not argued for.

statements.text: The revealed truths that lead to heaven are above our comprehension.
To undertake competently the examination of the revealed truths would need some special help from heaven and being more than man.
I should not presume to subject the revealed truths to the weakness of my reason.
Philosophy has been cultivated for many ages by the most distinguished men.
There is not a single matter within the sphere of philosophy that is not still in dispute.
A matter still disputed among learned men is not above doubt.

meta.note: Implicit. Descartes passes from 'still in dispute' to 'nothing above doubt' with a 'therefore'; this is the bridging principle that inference needs.

statements.text: Nothing in philosophy is above doubt.

meta.note: Established at I.12; II.13 restates it as 'philosophy, in which I found nothing certain'.

statements.text: I could not presume that my success in philosophy would be greater than that of others.
On a single matter, learned men may uphold many conflicting opinions.
Of the many conflicting opinions learned men may uphold on a single matter, only one can be true.
Whatever is only probable should be reckoned as well-nigh false.

meta.note: Reappears in Part IV as the rule to reject as absolutely false whatever admits the least ground for doubt.

statements.text: The other sciences borrow their principles from philosophy.
No solid superstructure can be raised by the other sciences on foundations so infirm as those of philosophy.
Neither the honor nor the gain offered by the sciences was enough to draw me to cultivate them.
I was not, thank Heaven, in a condition that compelled me to make merchandise of science to better my fortune.
Though I did not scorn glory like a cynic, I made very slight account of honor that could be gained only through fictitious titles.
I knew the worth of the false sciences well enough not to be deceived by an alchemist, an astrologer, a magician, or anyone professing to know what he does not.
I should abandon the study of letters entirely and seek no other science than the knowledge of myself or of the great book of the world.

meta.note: Descartes reports acting on this as soon as his age let him leave his instructors.

statements.text: When a man reasons about affairs that concern him personally, the outcome soon punishes him if he has judged wrongly.

A scholar's speculations on matters of no practical moment carry no consequences for him except to feed his vanity, the more so the further they depart from common sense, and requiring all the more ingenuity and art to be made probable.
There is much more truth in each man's reasonings about the affairs that concern him than in the speculations of a man of letters in his study.

meta.note: III.6 relies on it again, without restating it: living among men rather than among books is why he hoped to examine his opinions better by travelling, and why the nine years yielded more truth.

statements.text: I have always had an earnest desire to learn to distinguish the true from the false, so as to see clearly the right path in life and follow it with confidence.
I should spend my youth traveling, visiting courts and armies, mixing with men of every disposition and rank, testing myself, and above all reflecting on my experience.

meta.note: Descartes reports that he did exactly this for the remainder of his youth.

statements.text: Considering the manners of other men, I found scarcely any ground for settled conviction and hardly less contradiction among them than among the opinions of the philosophers.
Many things that seem extravagant and ridiculous to us are received and approved by common consent among other great nations.
I should not believe too firmly anything of whose truth I have been persuaded merely by example and custom.

meta.note: Stated at I.15 as the chief lesson of his travels. II.4 draws the descriptive counterpart (the ground of our opinions is custom and example) and relies on this rule tacitly to move from 'our opinions rest on custom' to 'I have no one to defer to'.

statements.text: Many of the errors that example and custom instil are powerful enough to darken our natural intelligence and largely incapacitate us from listening to reason.

meta.note: Characterises the errors shed at I.15; used in no inference.

statements.text: I gradually freed myself from many errors that darken our natural intelligence.
I should make myself the object of study and employ all the powers of my mind in choosing the paths I ought to follow.
My study of myself succeeded better than it would have had I never left my country or my books.
Detained by winter in Germany on my way back to the army, with no company, cares, or passions to distract me, I spent whole days shut up alone with my thoughts.

meta.note: The famous stove-heated room (the poele); Veitch renders it 'in seclusion'. Descartes was returning from the emperor's coronation. Biographical frame for Part II; used in no inference.

statements.text: Buildings one architect planned are more elegant than those many have patched; towns planned freely on an open plain are better laid out than cities grown piecemeal from villages.

meta.note: Piecemeal cities look arranged by chance rather than by reason, even though officers have always overseen public ornament: working with the materials of others makes high perfection hard to reach.

statements.text: There is seldom as much perfection in works composed of many parts by different hands as in those completed by a single master.

meta.note: Descartes states this first, as one of the first thoughts that came to him, and then offers buildings and cities as its observable instances.

statements.text: Nations whose laws were forced on them piecemeal by experience of particular crimes and disputes have less perfect institutions than those that followed one wise legislator from the start.
The constitution of the true religion, whose ordinances are derived from God, must be incomparably superior to that of every other.
Sparta was pre-eminent, though many of its laws taken singly were very strange and even opposed to good morals.
Sparta's pre-eminence was due not to the goodness of each of its laws but to their all coming from one man and tending to one end.
The book sciences of probable reasonings without demonstrations, being opinions of many massed together, are farther from truth than a man of good sense's simple inferences from his own experience.
We all pass through infancy before manhood and were long governed by our desires and by preceptors whose dictates often conflicted and were not always for the best.
It is almost impossible that our judgments are as correct and solid as they would be had our reason been mature from birth and always our only guide.
It is not customary to pull down all the houses of a town merely to rebuild them differently and make the streets more handsome.
A private individual often takes down his own house to rebuild it, and is sometimes forced to when it is in danger of falling or its foundations are insecure.
A state, or the body of the sciences and the schools, is like a whole town built by many hands; my own opinions are like a private house that is mine to rebuild.

meta.note: Implicit. Descartes moves straight from the town example to the state, the sciences, and his own opinions without stating the likeness; the whole inference of II.2 rests on it. II.3: 'the reformation of my own opinions, and basing them on a foundation wholly my own'.

statements.text: The principles on which my opinions have rested are ones I took upon trust in my youth, not ones I examined by reason.
A private individual should not try to reform a state, or the body of the sciences and the order of teaching in the schools, by overturning it to set it up amended.

meta.note: Descartes calls such a project 'preposterous'.

statements.text: I should sweep away all the opinions I have so far embraced, so as afterwards to admit better ones, or the same ones once they have passed the scrutiny of reason.

meta.note: II.3: he has never contemplated anything higher than reforming his own opinions and basing them on a foundation wholly his own. Part III presupposes this resolution ('my reason compelled me to suspend my judgement').

statements.text: Large bodies, once overthrown, are set up again only with great difficulty, are hard even to keep erect once seriously shaken, and their fall is always disastrous.
States have imperfections, as the diversity of constitutions shows, but custom has smoothed them, and they are almost always more tolerable than the change needed to remove them.

meta.note: Illustrated by the mountain highway worn smooth by use, which is better followed than a straighter path over rocks and precipices. Custom, he adds, corrected many defects that foresight could not have provided against.

statements.text: The difficulties I recognised in the undertaking of reforming my own opinions were not without remedy.
The difficulties of reforming my own opinions are not to be compared with those that attend even the slightest reformation of public affairs.
Those called by neither birth nor fortune to manage public affairs should not be forever projecting reforms of them.

meta.note: Descartes adds that he would not permit publication of this tract if he thought it could be suspected of such folly.

statements.text: The majority of men is made up of two classes: those who, over-confident in their own powers, are precipitate in their judgments, and those with sense or modesty enough to see that others surpass them in telling truth from error.
Those who are overconfident and precipitate, lacking the patience for orderly and circumspect thinking, will, if they once doubt their accustomed opinions, lose their way and wander for life.
Those with sense or modesty enough to see that others surpass them in telling truth from error should rather follow the opinions of such people than trust their own reason.
The design of stripping oneself of all past beliefs should not be undertaken by everyone; for most people it is more than they can safely imitate.

meta.note: Descartes allows that those God has endowed with more genius may attempt still more exalted designs; the warning is for 'the many'. He does not recommend that everyone imitate him.

statements.text: I would doubtless have belonged to the class that ought to defer to its betters, had I been taught by a single master or never known the diversity of opinion that has always prevailed among the most learned.
No opinion, however absurd or incredible, can be imagined that has not been maintained by some philosopher; I learned this already in my college days.

Many nations whose opinions are quite contrary to ours use their reason as well as or better than we do; the same mind raised among the Chinese would think differently than in France; fashions reverse within ten years.

meta.note: Three of the four observations of II.4 (the travels, the upbringing, the fashions), grouped because Descartes runs them together as one body of evidence.

statements.text: The ground of our opinions is far more custom and example than any certain knowledge.
A plurality of votes is no guarantee of truth where truth is at all hard to discover; there it is much more likely to be found by one than by many.

meta.note: Stated as an observation. It is the epistemic twin of the single-master principle of II.1 (single-author-works-more-perfect), though Descartes does not derive one from the other.

statements.text: I could select from the crowd no one whose opinions seemed worthy of being preferred to the rest.
I must rely on my own reason, rather than on the opinions of others, in the conduct of my life.

meta.note: Descartes: 'I found myself constrained, as it were, to use my own reason.'

statements.text: Like one walking alone in the dark, I should proceed so slowly and circumspectly that I at least guard against falling, and find the true method before dismissing any opinion.

meta.note: He did not dismiss summarily even the opinions that had crept in without reason, but first took time to understand the task and to find the method for whatever knowledge lay within his powers.

statements.text: Logic's syllogisms and most of its precepts serve to communicate what we already know, or to speak without judgment of what we do not, rather than to discover the unknown.

meta.note: 'Speaking without judgment of things of which we are ignorant' is his description of the art of Lully.

statements.text: Logic contains excellent precepts, but so many injurious or superfluous ones are mixed in that separating them is as hard as carving a Diana or Minerva from rough marble.
The ancients' analysis is so tied to figures that it fatigues the imagination; the moderns' algebra is so bound to rules and formulas that it confuses rather than cultivates the mind.

meta.note: Both, moreover, embrace only highly abstract matters of apparently no use. Logic, geometrical analysis and algebra were the three arts Descartes expected to contribute something to his design.

statements.text: I should seek some other method that comprises the advantages of logic, geometrical analysis, and algebra while being exempt from their defects.
A multitude of laws often only hampers justice; a state is best governed when it has few laws and these are rigidly administered.
In place of the great number of precepts of which logic is composed, four precepts will be perfectly sufficient for me, provided I never once fail to observe them.
I should take the firm and unwavering resolution never, in a single instance, to fail in observing my four precepts.
I should accept nothing as true that I do not clearly know to be so, admitting into my judgments only what is presented so clearly and distinctly that I cannot doubt it.

meta.note: That is: carefully avoid precipitancy and prejudice. Applied at III.6 in testing opinions by clear reasoning, at IV.1 in its strictest form as the method of doubt, and restated at VI.10 as a description of his practice.

statements.text: I should divide each difficulty I examine into as many parts as possible and as are needed to solve it properly.
I should conduct my thoughts in order, starting from the simplest and easiest objects and ascending step by step to the more complex, assigning an order even where none exists naturally.
I should in every case make my enumerations so complete and my reviews so general that I can be sure nothing is omitted.
Geometers reach the conclusions of their most difficult demonstrations by long chains of simple and easy reasonings.
All things man can know are connected like the geometers' chains; nothing is too remote or hidden to discover, provided we never take the false for true and keep the order of deduction.

meta.note: The two provisos are the first and third precepts restated.

statements.text: Of all who have so far sought truth in the sciences, only the mathematicians have found demonstrations, that is, certain and evident reasons.
The simplest and easiest objects to know, with which one must begin, are the very ones the mathematicians have examined.

meta.note: Veitch renders this 'such must have been the rule of their investigations'; the original says the starting objects are the same ones the mathematicians examined, which is what the next step (begin-with-mathematics) relies on, and the next sentence of II.11 (no intention 'of attempting to master all the particular sciences commonly denominated mathematics') confirms that the simplest objects meant are those of mathematics.

statements.text: I should begin with the examination of the simplest objects, those of mathematics, expecting only to accustom my mind to love truth and to dislike unsound reasoning.
However different their objects, all the sciences called mathematics agree in considering only the various relations or proportions among those objects.

I should consider proportions in the most general form possible, not referring them to any particular objects except those that most help in knowing them, and never restricting them to these, so that I can afterwards apply them to every class of objects where they hold.

meta.note: He did not intend to master all the particular sciences called mathematics.

statements.text: To understand these relations I must sometimes consider them one by one, and sometimes only bear them in mind or embrace many of them together.
Straight lines are the simplest objects and the most distinctly represented to my imagination and senses; the briefest possible symbols best hold many relations in memory at once.
I should view proportions as holding between straight lines when considering them one by one, and express them by the briefest symbols when holding many in mind together.
In this way I can borrow all that is best in geometrical analysis and in algebra, and correct the defects of each by the help of the other.
I have not restricted the method to any particular subject matter.
In two or three months of observing these precepts I solved questions I had thought very hard and, for the rest, determined how far and by what means solution was possible.

meta.note: Reported as an observed result; the argument into it records Descartes' own account of what produced it.

statements.text: Because I began with the simplest and most general truths, each truth I discovered served as a rule for discovering the ones that followed.
The truth on any particular point is one.

meta.note: Stated in passing as self-evident; it underwrites the claim that grasping the truth on a point exhausts what can be known about it.

statements.text: Whoever apprehends the truth on a point knows all that can be known about it, as a child who has added correctly by rule knows all that can be found about that sum.

meta.note: Offered so that his claim to have determined the extent of what could be solved will not seem vain.

statements.text: The method that teaches adherence to the true order and exact enumeration of all the conditions of what is sought includes everything that gives certitude to the rules of arithmetic.

The chief ground of my satisfaction with the method is the assurance of exercising my reason in all matters, if not perfectly, at least as well as I am able; and by its use my mind is becoming habituated to clearer and more distinct conceptions of its objects.

meta.note: 'The chief ground of my satisfaction with this method.'

statements.text: I can hope to apply the method to the difficulties of the other sciences with no less success than to those of algebra.
Before examining the difficulties of the other sciences, I must first try to establish the principles of philosophy.

meta.note: To attack all the sciences at once would be contrary to the order prescribed by the method.

statements.text: Establishing the principles of philosophy is of all inquiries the most important, and the one in which precipitancy and anticipation in judgment are most to be dreaded.
At that time I was only twenty-three years old.
I should not approach the principles of philosophy until I am more mature, and should first prepare by rooting out my errors, gathering varied experience, and practising my method.

meta.note: The preparation has three parts: eradicating the erroneous opinions accepted so far, amassing experience as material for reasoning, and continual exercise in the method to gain skill.

statements.text: Before rebuilding the house one lives in, it is not enough to pull it down, gather materials and draw a plan; one also needs another house to live in during the work.

meta.note: The governing analogy of Part III: the provisional morality is the temporary house.

statements.text: In action it frequently happens that no delay is permissible.

meta.note: Stated in III.3; the editor reads it as the unstated reason behind the aim of III.1 (no-delay-forbids-irresolution).

statements.text: I must not remain irresolute in my actions while my reason compels me to suspend judgement.
I should live from now on in the greatest possible happiness.

meta.note: Stated as an end in III.1 without argument; also the end that maxim 3 serves in III.4.

statements.text: While my opinions are under examination I should follow a provisional moral code of three or four maxims.
I should obey the laws and customs of my country.

meta.note: The first clause of maxim 1, stated without a separate reason.

statements.text: Because I intend to subject all my opinions to examination, I hold them for nothing in the meantime.
In the meantime I cannot do better than follow the opinions of the most judicious people.
There may be people among the Persians and the Chinese as judicious as any among ourselves.

meta.note: A concession, not a ground; used in no inference.

statements.text: It is most expedient to regulate one's practice by the opinions of the people one has to live among.

meta.note: 'Expediency seemed to dictate'; no further reason is given.

statements.text: I should regulate my practice by the opinions of the most judicious among the people I actually live with.
In the corruption of our manners, few people are disposed to say exactly what they believe.
The act of mind by which a thing is believed is different from the act by which we know that we believe it, and the one is often found without the other.
Very many people are not aware of what they really believe.
To learn what people really believe, I should attend to what they practise rather than to what they say.
All excess is generally vicious.

meta.note: Given parenthetically as the reason moderate opinions are probably the best.

statements.text: The most moderate opinions are always the most convenient for practice.
If I choose a moderate opinion and turn out to be wrong, I am less far from the truth than if I had chosen one extreme when the other was right.
Among opinions held in equal repute, I should always choose the most moderate and the farthest from extremes.
I find nothing on earth that is wholly superior to change.
I hope gradually to perfect my judgements, and not to let them deteriorate.
I should not bind myself to hold something good in the future merely because I approve of it now; that would be a grave sin against good sense.
Promises by which some part of our freedom is abridged belong among the extremes to be avoided.
I do not disapprove of laws that permit binding vows and contracts, to steady the weak-willed toward a good end or, for the security of commerce, even where the end is indifferent.

meta.note: A concession: his refusal of binding promises is personal, not a criticism of such laws; used in no inference.

statements.text: The truths of faith have always occupied the first place in my belief.
I should adhere firmly to the faith in which, by the grace of God, I was educated from childhood.

meta.note: The religious clause of maxim 1.

statements.text: I should obey my country's laws and customs, keep the religion I was raised in, and otherwise follow the most moderate opinions practised by the most judicious people around me.
Travellers lost in a forest should not wander about or stay put, but keep going one way as straight as possible, not changing course for slight reasons, even if chance chose it.

meta.note: The analogy for maxim 2.

statements.text: Travellers who keep a steady course, even one chosen by chance, will at least end up somewhere probably better than the middle of a forest.
When it is not in my power to determine what is true, I should act according to what is most probable.
Even when I see no greater probability in one opinion than in another, I should still choose one of them.

The reason that determined my choice, that when I cannot determine the truth and cannot delay I ought to act on the most probable or else choose, is itself very certain and true, whatever opinion I chose.

meta.note: 'The reason by which our choice has been determined is itself possessed of these qualities.'

statements.text: Once I have chosen a course, I should regard it, so far as practice is concerned, as no longer doubtful but manifestly true and certain.
I should be as firm and resolute in my actions as I can, holding to even the most doubtful opinions, once adopted, as steadfastly as if they were highly certain.

meta.note: IV.1 recalls this maxim ('as has been already said') only to set it aside: in the search for truth, the opposite procedure is called for.

statements.text: Feeble and uncertain minds lacking a clear principle of choice adopt a course one day as best, abandon it the next as the opposite, and are troubled by repentings and remorse.
My second maxim was enough to rid me of the repentings and pangs of remorse that disturb feeble and uncertain minds.
Except our own thoughts, there is nothing absolutely in our power.

meta.note: The Stoic premise on which maxim 3 rests; asserted, not argued.

statements.text: When we have done our best in things external to us, whatever we still fail in should be held, as regards us, absolutely impossible.
Our will naturally seeks only those objects which the understanding represents as in some way possible to attain.

meta.note: Psychological premise asserted without argument.

statements.text: If we regard all external goods as equally beyond our power, we will no more regret losing goods due to our birth than not owning the kingdoms of China.
Accustoming myself to the persuasion that only my thoughts are in my power seemed to me enough to stop me desiring anything I could not obtain, and so to make me content.
Certain philosophers of former times rose above the influence of fortune and, amid suffering and poverty, enjoyed a happiness their gods might have envied.

The secret of those philosophers' power lay chiefly in prolonged discipline and incessant meditation on the limits nature set to their power, which so convinced them that nothing was theirs but their thoughts that they ceased to desire anything else and gained absolute sway over their thoughts.
However many favours nature and fortune heap on a person, without this philosophy he can never command the realization of all his desires.
Those who have absolute command of their thoughts have ground to count themselves richer, more powerful, freer and happier than people favoured by fortune who lack this philosophy.
Prolonged discipline and frequently repeated meditation are needed to accustom the mind to view all things in this light.

meta.note: A confessed qualification of maxim 3, and the thing in which the philosophers' secret chiefly consisted.

statements.text: I should always try to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world, holding that only my thoughts are absolutely in my power.
I should review the different occupations of men and choose the best one for myself.

meta.note: The aim announced at the start of III.5, completing the moral code.

statements.text: Since I began applying my method it has given me satisfaction so intense that I believe none more perfect or more innocent can be enjoyed in this life.
By my method I daily discover truths that seem to me of some importance and of which other men are generally ignorant, and this gratification leaves me indifferent to every other object.
I should continue in my present occupation, devoting my whole life to cultivating my reason and advancing as far as I can in the knowledge of truth by my method.
God has endowed each of us with some light of reason by which to distinguish truth from error.

meta.note: Compare the equal distribution of good sense in I.1; here given a theological grounding.

statements.text: I should not rest satisfied for a moment with the opinions of others unless I have resolved to examine them by my own judgement as soon as I am qualified.

meta.note: The condition under which maxim 1 is acceptable.

statements.text: I could not have acted on doubtful opinions without scruple had I supposed that I was thereby forfeiting any chance of attaining more accurate ones.

meta.note: The condition under which maxim 2 is acceptable.

statements.text: I could not have restrained my desires, nor remained content, had I not followed a path on which I was sure of attaining all the knowledge and true good within my reach.

meta.note: The condition under which maxim 3 is acceptable.

statements.text: The three maxims of my provisional code were founded solely on my design of continuing to instruct myself.
We neither seek nor shun anything except insofar as our understanding represents it as good or bad.

meta.note: Intellectualist premise about motivation; asserted without argument.

statements.text: All that is necessary for right action is right judgement, and for the best action the most correct judgement.
The most correct judgement brings the acquisition of all the virtues and everything else truly valuable within our reach, and assurance of that acquisition cannot fail to make us content.
Having placed my maxims in reserve along with the truths of faith, I may now freely set about ridding myself of all my remaining opinions.

meta.note: A permission rather than an obligation, hence normative; the temporary house is in place, so demolition may begin.

statements.text: I could carry out the examination of my opinions better by mixing with mankind than by staying shut up in the retreat where these thoughts occurred to me.

meta.note: Stated as a hope; III.6 gives no reason for it. The link from the I.14 principle is reconstructed (travel-hope-from-practical-truth).

statements.text: I should resume travelling and examine my opinions among men, as a spectator rather than an actor in the world's affairs.

meta.note: Descartes reports doing so for nine years, setting out again before the winter was over.

statements.text: In every matter I made it my business to reflect particularly on what might fairly be doubted and prove a source of error.
I gradually rooted out from my mind all the errors that had crept into it.
The sceptics doubt only in order to doubt, and seek nothing beyond uncertainty itself.
My design in doubting was solely to find ground for assurance, casting aside the loose earth and sand so as to reach the rock or clay.
In thus rooting out my errors by seeking what could be doubted I was not imitating the sceptics.
I sought to discover the falsehood or uncertainty of the propositions I examined by clear and certain reasonings, not by feeble conjectures.
Nothing I examined was so doubtful that it failed to yield some conclusion of adequate certainty, even if only that the matter contained nothing certain.
In pulling down an old house, we usually keep the ruins to help build the new one.

meta.note: Analogy.

statements.text: In destroying the opinions I judged ill-founded, I made many observations and gained experience that I later used in establishing more certain ones.

Throughout these years I continued to exercise my method, conducting all my thoughts by its rules and setting aside hours for mathematical problems and for questions of other sciences made almost mathematical.

meta.note: Questions of other sciences were made 'almost mathematical' by detaching them from principles of inadequate certainty.

statements.text: Though outwardly living like those who pass their lives agreeably and innocently, I made greater progress in the knowledge of truth than I might perhaps have made from books alone or the company of scholars.
Nine years passed before I reached any determinate judgement on the disputes of the learned or began to seek the principles of a philosophy more certain than the common one.
Many men of the highest genius had formerly undertaken this inquiry and, as it seemed to me, without success.
Founding a philosophy more certain than the common one is, as I came to imagine, a work of very great difficulty.
It was commonly rumoured that I had already completed the inquiry into the principles of philosophy.
If my conversation fed the rumour, it was because I confessed my ignorance more freely than others and gave my reasons for doubting, not because I boasted of any philosophy.

meta.note: Descartes' guess at the rumour's origin; used in no inference.

statements.text: I am of a disposition that makes me unwilling to be esteemed different from what I really am.
I should try by every means to make myself worthy of the reputation accorded to me.
Given the difficulty of the inquiry I would perhaps not have ventured on it so soon, had I not heard it rumoured that I had already completed it.
To pursue this inquiry I need to be free from interruption by my acquaintances.

meta.note: Implicit: it is the only reason given for leaving every place where acquaintances could interrupt him.

statements.text: In this country the armies serve only to secure the inhabitants' peace, and amid a busy crowd minding its own affairs I can enjoy every convenience of the most populous cities while living as solitary as in a desert.

meta.note: 'This country' is Holland, not named in the text.

statements.text: I should remove to a place where no acquaintance can interrupt me, namely this country.

meta.note: Descartes reports acting on this eight years before writing; 'this country' is Holland, not named in the text.

statements.text: My first meditations are so metaphysical and so uncommon that they may not be acceptable to everyone.

meta.note: A concession Descartes states before giving his reason; used in no inference.

statements.text: It must be possible to determine whether the foundations I have laid are sufficiently secure.

meta.note: Implicit. IV.1 says 'that it may be determined whether the foundations that I have laid are sufficiently secure, I find myself in a measure constrained to advert to them'; that they must be open to judgment is not stated.

statements.text: I am constrained to recount my first meditations, despite their strangeness, so that it can be judged whether my foundations are sufficiently secure.
My aim in these meditations is solely the search for truth: to discover whether anything in my beliefs is wholly indubitable.
I ought to reject as absolutely false every opinion in which I can imagine the least ground for doubt, to see whether anything wholly indubitable remains.

meta.note: The method of doubt. Descartes stresses it is a procedure for the search for truth only, the opposite of the rule he follows in practice.

statements.text: Our senses sometimes deceive us.
I suppose that nothing exists as the senses present it to us.

meta.note: A deliberate supposition adopted under the method of doubt, not a belief.

statements.text: Some men err in reasoning and fall into paralogisms even on the simplest matters of geometry.
I am as open to error as anyone else.

meta.note: VI.5 restates it: 'I recognise my extreme liability to error, and scarce ever trust to the first thoughts which occur to me.'

statements.text: I reject as false all the reasonings I had previously taken for demonstrations.

meta.note: A supposition adopted under the method of doubt.

statements.text: The very same thoughts we have when awake can also occur when we are asleep, when none of them is true, and dreams are often no less vivid and distinct.
I suppose that everything that has ever entered my mind while awake has no more truth than the illusions of my dreams.

meta.note: A supposition adopted under the method of doubt.

statements.text: I doubt: I am uncertain of the truth of many things.
To doubt is to think.

meta.note: Implicit: Descartes moves from 'I thought to doubt' and 'I wished to think that all was false' straight to 'I think'. Surfaced because the cogito rests on it.

statements.text: I am thinking; even my attempt to suppose that everything is false is itself an act of thought.
In order to think, it is necessary to exist.

meta.note: Descartes says he sees this 'very clearly' and that it is the sole ground of the cogito's certainty (IV.3). Treated as self-evident, never argued for.

statements.text: I think, therefore I am: I exist.
The truth 'I think, therefore I am' is so certain and evident that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, that the sceptics could allege can shake it.
I may without scruple accept 'I think, therefore I am' as the first principle of the philosophy I am seeking.
I can suppose that I have no body and that there is no world and no place in which I exist.
I cannot suppose that I do not exist.
If I had merely ceased to think, I would have had no reason to believe that I existed, even if everything else I had ever imagined were real.
What I can suppose myself to exist without does not belong to my essence; what I cannot suppose away while I exist is my whole essence.

meta.note: Implicit. IV.2 moves from what can and cannot be supposed to what I am; this bridging principle is never stated but is what licenses the move from doubt to essence.

statements.text: I am a substance whose whole essence or nature consists only in thinking.
In order to exist, I need no place and depend on no material thing.
The 'I', that is, the mind by which I am what I am, is wholly distinct from the body.

meta.note: V.3 refers back to it: the soul is that part of us distinct from the body whose nature consists in thinking.

statements.text: The mind is more easily known than the body.
Even if the body did not exist, the mind would still continue to be all that it is.
Since I have found one proposition that I know to be true, I can also discover what its certainty consists in.

meta.note: Methodological premise stated briefly at the start of IV.3; it is what turns the cogito into a source for a general criterion of truth.

statements.text: Nothing assures me of the truth of 'I think, therefore I am' except that I see very clearly that in order to think one must exist.
Whatever we conceive very clearly and distinctly is true.

meta.note: The criterion of truth. Derived from the cogito in IV.3 and then, in IV.7, said to be certain only because God exists; the file records both justifications, which together form the Cartesian circle. Part V rests the certainty of the laws of nature on it.

statements.text: There is some difficulty in rightly determining which things we conceive distinctly.

meta.note: Descartes' own caveat on the criterion, which he does not resolve in Part IV; used in no inference.

statements.text: It is a greater perfection to know than to doubt.

meta.note: Descartes says he 'clearly saw' this.

statements.text: My being is not wholly perfect.
I have in me the idea of something more perfect than myself.
My ideas of the sky, earth, light, heat and the like contain nothing superior to me; they could come from my own nature, or from its imperfection if false.

meta.note: The contrast case: ordinary ideas need no source beyond myself, which is why the idea of a more perfect being is special. A contrast, not a premise; used in no inference.

statements.text: It is manifestly impossible for anything to proceed from nothing.
It is no less repugnant that the more perfect should be an effect of, or depend on, the less perfect than that something should proceed from nothing.
Any idea I have was received either from nothing, from myself, or from some other nature.

meta.note: Implicit. This is the enumeration of possible sources over which the elimination in IV.4 runs ('it but remained that...'); Descartes never states it as a premise.

statements.text: My idea of a nature more perfect than myself was placed in me by a nature that really is more perfect, namely God.
God, a being that is wholly perfect and possesses every perfection of which I can form an idea, exists.

meta.note: Reached by three separate arguments in Part IV: from the source of the idea of perfection, from my own dependence, and from the idea of a Perfect Being containing existence. Part V builds on it as one of its two first principles.

statements.text: I know of some perfections that I do not possess.
Had I existed alone and given myself the little perfection I possess, I could equally have given myself all the perfection I lack: infinity, eternity, immutability, omniscience, omnipotence.

meta.note: The counterfactual on which the dependence argument turns. It quietly assumes that a being able to give itself a perfection would have done so.

statements.text: I am not the only being; I depend on a more perfect Being from whom I have received everything I possess.
God possesses every perfection of which I can form an idea, and nothing that marks an imperfection is in him.

meta.note: Includes that God is veracious: falsity is an imperfection (IV.7, IV.8). Part V says the laws of nature were demonstrated from no other principle than the infinite perfection of God.

statements.text: I myself would be happy to be free of doubt, inconstancy and sadness.
Whatever I would gladly be rid of is a mark of imperfection.

meta.note: Implicit. Descartes' test for imperfection.

statements.text: Doubt, inconstancy, sadness and the like cannot be found in God.
Even if I am dreaming and all I see or imagine is false, I cannot deny that the ideas of sensible and corporeal things are really in my thoughts.

meta.note: Raises the question, answered in the same paragraph, whether God might be corporeal as well as intelligent. The occasion of the question, not a premise; used in no inference.

statements.text: All composition is evidence of dependency.
A state of dependency is manifestly a state of imperfection.
Whatever is not wholly perfect is in a state of dependency.

meta.note: Implicit. The converse of dependency-is-imperfection; IV.4 asserts that imperfect natures depend on God without stating the principle that carries the step.

statements.text: God is not compounded of the intelligent and the corporeal natures.
If there are any bodies, intelligences or other natures not wholly perfect, their existence depends on God's power so that they could not subsist without him for a single moment.
The object of the geometers is a continuous body or space indefinitely extended in length, breadth and depth, divisible into parts of various figures and sizes, and movable in every way.

meta.note: Scene-setting for IV.5; used in no inference.

statements.text: The great certainty accorded by common consent to geometrical demonstrations rests solely on their being clearly conceived according to my rule.
Nothing in a geometrical demonstration assures me that its object exists: I perceive that a triangle's angles equal two right angles without perceiving that any triangle exists.

meta.note: The disanalogy with the idea of a Perfect Being (IV.5); a contrast, not a premise, so used in no inference.

statements.text: Existence is comprised in the idea of a Perfect Being just as having angles equal to two right angles is comprised in the idea of a triangle, or even more clearly.

meta.note: Descartes reports this as something he 'found' on examining the idea; it is the premise of the ontological argument.

statements.text: It is at least as certain that God, the Perfect Being, exists as any demonstration of geometry can be.
Imagination is a mode of thinking limited to material objects.
The philosophers of the schools accept as a maxim that there is nothing in the understanding which was not previously in the senses.
The ideas of God and of the soul have never been in the senses.

meta.note: Descartes calls this 'certain'.

statements.text: Those who find it hard to know God and the soul do so because they consider everything by way of imagination, so that whatever is not imaginable seems to them unintelligible.
The ideas of God and of the soul, which were never in the senses, refute the maxim of the schools that there is nothing in the understanding which was not previously in the senses.
Neither our imagination nor our senses can give us assurance of anything unless our understanding intervenes.

The certainty of geometry, and of every other proposition besides the existence of God and of the soul, depends on God existing, being a Perfect Being, and being the source of all we possess, so that no falsity can come from him.
We have a moral assurance that we have a body and that stars and an earth exist, so strong that doubting them appears extravagant.

meta.note: A concession, not a premise: moral assurance is what the dream doubt overrides, falling short of the metaphysical certainty Descartes is after; used in no inference.

statements.text: That we have a body and that stars and an earth exist is less certain than the existence of God and of the soul.
Any reason for holding our waking thoughts true rather than our dreams must rest on the rule that what we clearly and distinctly conceive is true.

meta.note: Implicit. IV.7 offers the criterion's dependence on God as the reason no answer to the dream doubt can avoid presupposing God; the premise that every such answer rests on the criterion is not stated.

statements.text: No reason can suffice to remove the doubt that dreams cast on our waking thoughts unless it presupposes the existence of God.
The rule that whatever we clearly and distinctly conceive is true is certain only because God exists, is a Perfect Being, and is the source of all we possess.

meta.note: Descartes adds the contrapositive: without knowing this, no idea however clear and distinct would give assurance of its truth.

statements.text: When our ideas contain some falsity, it is only in so far as they are confused and obscure and thus proceed from nothing, because we are not wholly perfect.
It is no less repugnant that falsity or imperfection should proceed from God than that truth or perfection should proceed from nothing.

meta.note: God is no deceiver.

statements.text: I ought not in the slightest degree to call the truth of my waking thoughts into question on account of the illusions of my dreams.
If someone had a very distinct idea even while asleep, as a geometer discovering a new demonstration, his being asleep would not tell against its truth.
We are often deceived by our senses when awake, as when those with jaundice see everything yellow, or distant stars and bodies appear much smaller than they are.
The ordinary error of dreams, representing objects as our external senses do, is not prejudicial, since it rightly leads us to suspect the ideas of sense.
Whether awake or asleep, I should never let myself be persuaded of the truth of anything except on the evidence of my reason, not of my imagination or senses.
Reason does not dictate that what we see or imagine exists as we see it: the sun is not the size it appears, and an imagined chimaera need not exist.

meta.note: Illustration of accept-only-on-evidence-of-reason; used in no inference.

statements.text: All our ideas or notions contain some truth.
Our reasonings are never so clear or so complete during sleep as when we are awake, although the acts of imagination may then be as lively and distinct or more so.
Since our partial imperfection means not all our thoughts can be true, those that possess truth must be found in our waking experience rather than in our dreams.

Supposing no principle beyond the one used to demonstrate God and the soul, and accepting nothing less certain than geometry, I deduced a chain of truths resolving the principal difficulties of philosophy.
God has established certain laws in nature.
God has impressed on our minds such notions of these laws that, after sufficient reflection, we cannot doubt them.
The laws of nature are exactly observed in everything that exists or takes place in the world.

meta.note: Descartes adds that by considering how these laws are concatenated he discovered many truths more useful and important than all he had learned before.

statements.text: To exhibit the whole chain of truths I would have to treat many questions in dispute among the learned.
I do not wish to be embroiled in disputes with the learned.
I should refrain from exhibiting the whole chain of truths here and only mention in general what they are.

meta.note: He leaves it to the more judicious to decide whether a fuller account would serve the public advantage.

statements.text: Light proceeds almost wholly from the sun and the fixed stars, crosses the immense spaces of the heavens in an instant, and is reflected by the planets, comets and the earth.

meta.note: This is also why the withheld treatise was organised around light: sun and stars produce it, the heavens transmit it, planets and earth reflect it, terrestrial bodies are coloured, transparent or luminous, and man is its spectator.

statements.text: In my fable I suppose that God has now created, somewhere in imaginary space, enough matter to compose a world, agitated it into utter chaos, and thereafter merely lent nature his ordinary concurrence under the laws he had established.

meta.note: A supposition, not an assertion about the actual world: Descartes explicitly declines to conclude that our world was made this way.

statements.text: This matter has none of the forms or qualities debated in the schools, nothing not so natural to our minds that no one could imagine being ignorant of it.

meta.note: Descartes says that, so described, nothing is clearer or more intelligible than this matter except what was said of God and the soul.

statements.text: Even had God created other worlds, there could be none in which these laws of nature were not observed.
By these laws alone, most of the chaotic matter must arrange itself as heavens, while other parts compose an earth, planets, comets, a sun and fixed stars.
Nothing observable in the heavens or stars of our system must not, or at least may not, appear precisely alike in the system I described.
Even without weight, the earth's parts tend to its centre; the heavens and moon cause tides and an east-west current; mountains, seas, rivers, metals, plants and all mixed bodies form naturally.

meta.note: Descartes expressly supposed that God gave the earth's matter no weight, and still derived the tendency of its parts to the centre.

statements.text: Besides the stars, I know of nothing but fire that produces light; its nature explains heat without light and light without heat, colours, liquefying and hardening, burning to ash, and the making of glass from ashes.

meta.note: He singles out the transmutation of ashes into glass as being as wonderful as anything in nature.

statements.text: It is much more likely that God made this world at first such as it was to be than that it arose in the manner I described.

meta.note: His stated caveat on the fable: he does not conclude that our world was created that way; used in no inference.

statements.text: The action by which God now sustains the world is the same as that by which he created it.

meta.note: Asserted in V.2 as certain and as an opinion commonly received among theologians; Descartes gives no argument for it there. The file supplies a reconstructed link from the continuous dependence of imperfect natures on God (IV.4).

statements.text: Had God begun the world as mere chaos, the laws of nature and his concurrence could in time have made material things as we now observe them, without discredit to creation.
The nature of material things is much more easily conceived when seen coming gradually into existence than when considered only as produced at once in a finished state.
By speaking only of what would happen in a new world I can throw the disputed subjects into the shade and express my judgement freely, without having to adopt or refute the opinions of the learned.
I should leave the learned to their disputes and speak only of what would happen in a new world.

meta.note: Stated in V.2 as a resolution ('I resolved').

statements.text: In the treatise I suppose that God formed a body exactly like ours from the matter I described, placing in it no rational, vegetative or sensitive soul, but only a fire without light kindled in the heart.

meta.note: Adopted because he did not yet know enough to deduce animals and man from their causes as he had the rest. The fire in the heart is said to be no different from the heat in damp heaped hay or in fermenting new wine.

statements.text: Such a body would have exactly all the functions that exist in us independently of any power of thinking.
The functions that exist in us independently of any power of thinking owe nothing at all to the soul, that part of us distinct from the body whose nature consists in thinking.
In the functions that owe nothing to the soul, the animals that lack reason wholly resemble us.

meta.note: Added in passing in V.3; used in no inference.

statements.text: In such a body I could find none of the functions that depend on thought alone and belong to us as men.
As soon as I supposed God had created a rational soul and joined it to this body in a particular manner, I found the functions that belong to us as men.
A real man is a body of this kind together with a rational soul created by God and united to it.
The motion of the heart and arteries is the first and most general motion observed in animals, and explaining it affords the means of readily determining what to think of all the rest.

meta.note: His reason for choosing the heart as the specimen of the mechanical account of the body.

statements.text: I should explain the motion of the heart and arteries as the specimen of how I handled the animal body.
The heart has two cavities: the right joins the hollow vein and the arterial vein to the lungs; the left joins the venous artery from the lungs and the great artery.

meta.note: The great artery sends branches over the whole body. He notes the arterial vein is really an artery and the venous artery really a vein, and that the two inlet vessels widen into the auricles before entering the heart.

statements.text: Eleven small valves at the four orifices let blood enter each cavity from the inlet vessels and leave into the arterial vein and great artery, but never flow back.

meta.note: Three valves at each round orifice and two at the oval orifice of the venous artery; he says the shape of the orifice is the only reason needed for the number.

statements.text: The great artery and the arterial vein are of much harder and firmer texture than the venous artery and the hollow vein.
There is always more heat in the heart than in any other part of the body.
Any liquid allowed to fall drop by drop into a highly heated vessel at once expands and dilates.
The heat of the heart causes any drop of blood entering its cavities to expand and dilate rapidly.
Blood enters the empty cavities, is rarefied by the heat, expands the heart, shuts the inlet valves and opens the outlet valves; then it cools, the heart contracts, and the cycle repeats.

meta.note: Descartes' own (non-Harveian) account of why the heart moves: rarefaction of blood by heat, not muscular contraction. He adds that the auricles, through which the blood enters, contract when the heart expands. V.7 calls this 'the true cause of the motion of the blood' and offers several confirmations, recorded here as separate arguments into this statement.

statements.text: The heart's motion follows as necessarily from the visible arrangement of its parts, its felt heat and the nature of blood as a clock's motion from its weights and wheels.
A moderately tight ligature above the place where a vein is opened makes blood flow more copiously, whereas a ligature below it, or a very tight one above, does the contrary.

meta.note: From the ordinary experience of surgeons.

statements.text: The arteries lie deeper than the veins, and the blood coming from the heart passes through them toward the hand with greater force than it returns through the veins.
There must be passages toward the extremities through which blood comes from the arteries into the veins.
Small valves disposed along the veins let blood return from the extremities to the heart but not pass from the middle of the body toward the extremities.
All the blood in the body can flow out in a very short time through a single cut artery, even one tied near the heart and cut between heart and ligature.
Blood received by the arteries from the heart passes through small passages into the veins and returns to the heart, so that its course is a perpetual circulation.

meta.note: Credited to 'a physician of England' (William Harvey), who Descartes says was first to teach it.

statements.text: The blood in the veins is never exhausted by flowing continually into the heart, and the arteries never become too full.
The rules of mechanics are the same as the rules of nature.

meta.note: Stated in passing while explaining the animal spirits; it underwrites the whole mechanical treatment of the body.

statements.text: Blood from the arteries is thinner, more vivid and warmer than blood from the veins, and this difference is marked only near the heart.
The left cavity of the heart and the great artery are wider and larger than the right cavity and the arterial vein.
Heat is communicated to the members by the blood, which is heated anew each time it passes through the heart and thence diffused over the whole body.
The true use of respiration is to bring fresh air into the lungs to thicken the blood rarefied in the right ventricle before it enters the left cavity.
Animals without lungs have only one cavity in the heart, and unborn children, who cannot use their lungs, have a hole and a tube by which blood bypasses them.
Digestion, the making of blood from food, and nutrition are all explained by the heat and rarefied blood the heart sends through the arteries.

meta.note: Nutrition: the rarefied blood leaves some of its parts in each member according to the size and shape of the pores, as variously perforated sieves sort grain.

statements.text: The animal spirits, like a very subtle wind or pure flame, ascend from the heart to the brain and pass through the nerves into the muscles, moving all the members.
Waking, sleep and dreams, sense impressions, hunger and thirst, common sense, memory, fantasy, and movements suited to objects can all arise in such a body apart from the will.
Human-made automata perform a great variety of movements with few pieces compared with the multitude of bones, muscles, nerves and vessels in an animal body.
The animal body is a machine made by the hands of God, incomparably better arranged and capable of more admirable movements than any machine of human invention.
If there were machines with the organs and outward form of an ape or any other irrational animal, we could have no means of knowing they differed in nature from those animals.
Reason is a universal instrument available on every occasion, whereas organs need a particular arrangement for each particular action.

meta.note: The stated ground of the second test (V.7) and, by reconstruction, of the first test and of the claim that the soul cannot come from matter.

statements.text: No machine could arrange words or signs variously so as to reply appositely to whatever is said in its presence, as even the dullest men can.

meta.note: The first test. Descartes concedes a machine could emit words, even words answering to the action of objects on its organs.

statements.text: A machine, though it might do many things better than we, would fail in others, revealing that it acts not from knowledge but from the disposition of its organs.

meta.note: The second test.

statements.text: Machines with the form of our bodies, imitating our actions as far as morally possible, would still fail two most certain tests that show they are not really men.
No man is so dull and stupid, not even an idiot, that he cannot join words together to make his thoughts understood.
No animal, however perfect or well circumstanced, can join words or signs to declare its thoughts.
Magpies and parrots can utter words yet not show they understand them, while men born deaf and dumb, lacking the organs of speech, invent signs to make their thoughts known.
The inability of animals to speak does not arise from lack of organs.
Very little reason is needed to be able to speak, and within a species of animals, as among men, some individuals are more capable and more teachable than others.
The brutes have not merely less reason than man but none at all.
The soul of the brutes is of a nature wholly different from ours.
The natural movements that indicate the passions can be imitated by machines as well as manifested by animals.
The natural movements that express the passions must not be confounded with speech.
Animals are endowed with many organs analogous to ours.
The brutes do not, as some of the ancients thought, speak a language that we merely fail to understand.
Many animals show more skill than we in certain actions yet none at all in many others.
It is nature that acts in animals according to the disposition of their organs, not reason.
The rational soul cannot in any way be derived from the power of matter, as the other things I described are.
The rational soul must be expressly created by God.
Whatever exists is either produced by matter acting under the laws of nature or expressly created by God.

meta.note: Implicit: Descartes moves straight from 'cannot be educed from matter' to 'must be expressly created', which needs this exhaustive disjunction.

statements.text: A soul lodged in the human body merely as a pilot in a ship could at most move its members, but could not have sensations and appetites like ours.
We have sensations and appetites that are truly our own.

meta.note: Implicit: the pilot-in-a-ship argument only works if we in fact have sensations and appetites, which a merely piloting soul could not have.

statements.text: The soul must be joined and united to the body more closely than a pilot to a ship, so as to have sensations and appetites and thus constitute a real man.
If the soul of brutes were of the same nature as ours, we would have nothing to hope for or fear after this life, any more than flies and ants.

meta.note: A conditional he asserts; it presupposes that the souls of brutes perish with their bodies.

statements.text: Believing that there is nothing to hope for or fear after this life leads feeble minds astray from the path of virtue.

meta.note: Implicit in his ranking of the brute-soul error beside atheism as most powerful in leading feeble minds from virtue.

statements.text: After atheism, no error is more powerful in leading feeble minds from the straight path of virtue than supposing the soul of brutes is of the same nature as ours.

meta.note: He treats atheism as already sufficiently refuted in Part IV.

statements.text: I should treat the subject of the soul at considerable length, because it is of the greatest moment.
The soul is of a nature wholly independent of the body.
The soul is not liable to die with the body.
No other causes are observed capable of destroying the soul.
The soul is immortal.

meta.note: Stated cautiously: 'we are naturally led thence to judge that it is immortal.'

statements.text: Persons to whom I greatly defer, whose authority over my actions is almost that of my reason over my thoughts, have condemned a doctrine in physics recently published by another.

meta.note: Neither the authorities nor the author are named; the reference is to the condemnation of Galileo in 1633.

statements.text: Before their censure I had observed nothing in that doctrine prejudicial to religion or the state, and therefore nothing that would have prevented me from expressing it in writing, had reason persuaded me of its truth.

meta.note: He does not say he held the doctrine, only that he had found nothing objectionable in it.

statements.text: I have always taken great care not to believe new opinions without the most certain demonstrations, and not to express anything that might harm anyone.

meta.note: Concession stated alongside the fear of VI.1 ('notwithstanding the great care...'), not a premise of it; derived from II.7 by the reconstructed link care-from-precept-and-rule.

statements.text: Some of my own doctrines may likewise have departed from the truth, despite all my care.
I should not publish doctrines that I have reason to fear may be false or prejudicial to religion or the state.

meta.note: Implicit: the mere fear that some doctrine may be in error is treated as sufficient to alter the purpose of publishing, which presupposes this rule.

statements.text: I should alter my purpose of publishing my treatise, and not now put it into the hands of a printer as I had intended.

meta.note: The immediate effect of the fear of error; the resolve never to publish in his lifetime comes only in VI.4 and VI.8.

statements.text: My inclination has always been hostile to writing books, and it readily supplied further reasons to excuse me from publishing.

meta.note: Descartes' own account of why the considerations of VI.4-7 occurred to him; a motive, not a premise, so used in no inference.

statements.text: I have never made much account of what has proceeded from my own mind.
So long as my method served only to settle speculative difficulties and to regulate my own conduct, I was under no obligation to publish anything about it.
In matters of conduct everyone is so full of his own wisdom that there would be as many reformers as heads if all were allowed to mend the manners of others.
Only those whom God has made rulers of his people, or given the grace and zeal to be prophets, may take upon themselves to reform the conduct of others.

meta.note: Echoes the refusal in II.3 to approve meddlers who project public reforms.

statements.text: Although my speculations greatly pleased me, I believed that others had theirs, which perhaps pleased them still more.
Having tried my general notions of physics on particular difficulties, I saw how far they can carry us and how much they differ from the principles employed until now.
Everyone is bound by a law to promote, as far as in him lies, the general good of mankind; to be useful to no one is really to be worthless.

meta.note: Stated as a law binding on all; not argued for.

statements.text: I cannot keep my general notions of physics concealed without sinning grievously against the law that binds us to promote, as far as in us lies, the general good of mankind.

meta.note: VI.4-8 then defer this for the physics itself: publication is withheld during his lifetime and the duty is discharged toward posterity by writing the results as if for publication (withhold-physics-to-serve-posterity, write-results-as-if-publishing); the tension is Descartes' own.

statements.text: By my principles it is possible to reach knowledge highly useful in life and, in place of the speculative philosophy of the schools, to discover a practical one.
Knowing the force and action of all bodies around us as distinctly as artisans know their crafts, we could apply them to every use and become the lords and possessors of nature.

meta.note: The bodies he lists are fire, water, air, the stars, the heavens and all other bodies that surround us. Veitch has 'lords and possessors'; the id keeps the familiar 'masters', which renders the French maitres.

statements.text: Mastery of nature is to be desired, both for inventing countless arts that would let us enjoy the fruits of the earth without toil, and above all for preserving health.
The preservation of health is without doubt the first and fundamental of all the blessings of this life.

meta.note: Asserted as beyond doubt and not argued for; the value premise behind both the desirability of mastering nature and the choice of medicine as life's work.

statements.text: The mind is intimately dependent on the condition and arrangement of the organs of the body.
