If any means can ever be found to make men wiser and more ingenious than hitherto, it must be sought in medicine.
Medicine as it now exists contains few things of remarkable utility; even its practitioners admit that all now known in it is almost nothing beside what remains to be discovered.
With sufficient knowledge of their causes and of the remedies nature provides, we could free ourselves from countless maladies of body and mind, and perhaps even from the debility of age.
I should devote whatever time I have left to live to no other occupation than seeking a knowledge of nature from which more certain rules of medicine can be deduced.

meta.note: Made as a public declaration in VI.12, explicitly without any promise about future progress.

statements.text: I have found a path such that whoever follows it must inevitably reach the knowledge sought, unless hindered by the shortness of life or the want of experiments.

meta.note: The two impediments named here drive the whole case for publishing.

statements.text: If each begins where those before him left off, connecting the lives and labours of many, we can collectively proceed much farther than any one could alone.
The most effectual provision against the shortness of life and the want of experiments is to communicate faithfully all I have found and incite abler men to carry the work farther.
I ought to communicate to the public all the little I have found, and incite men of superior genius to contribute experiments and discoveries of their own.

meta.note: This is the case FOR publishing, which VI.4-8 then qualify: the physics is withheld and only the Discourse with specimen essays is published.

statements.text: Experiments become always more necessary the further one advances in knowledge.
Uncommon phenomena often only mislead us so long as the causes of ordinary ones are unknown, and the circumstances they depend on are almost always so special and minute as to be very hard to detect.
At the outset of inquiry one should use only what is spontaneously presented to the senses rather than concern oneself with rare and recondite phenomena.
I first sought the first causes of all things from God and the innate germs of truth alone, then deduced from them the commonest effects: heavens, stars, earth, water, air, fire, minerals.

meta.note: The order of his physics; the commonest effects are called the simplest and easiest to know.

statements.text: The particular bodies on earth cannot be distinguished from the countless others God might have made, nor applied to our use, unless we rise to causes through effects by many particular experiments.
I have never observed anything that I could not satisfactorily explain by the principles I have discovered.
Nature is so ample and my principles so simple and general that almost every effect can be deduced from them in several ways; my greatest difficulty is finding which way is actual.
The only way to discover which mode an effect actually depends on is by experiments whose result would differ according to which explanation is the true one.
The experiments required are so many that neither my own hands nor my income, though it were a thousand times larger, would suffice for them all.

meta.note: VI.7 restates this as: one man alone is not equal to making all the experiments.

statements.text: According as I have the means of making more or fewer experiments, I shall make greater or less progress in the knowledge of nature.

A treatise that clearly exhibited the advantage accruing to the public would induce all who truly have the common good at heart to communicate the experiments they had already made and to assist me in those that remain.

meta.note: What he had hoped the withheld treatise would do; VI.7 later argues that such help is mostly unusable.

statements.text: I should not publish during my lifetime my treatise on physics, nor any work so general that the principles of my physics could be understood from it.

meta.note: The treatise is the physics finished three years earlier and summarised in Part V. Two lines of argument reach this: husbanding time for posterity (VI.4), and the considerations of VI.4-7 taken together (VI.8); the fear of VI.1 only suspended the printing (see suspend-publication-of-treatise).

statements.text: I ought to keep committing to writing every result I judge of moment as soon as I have tested it, with the same care as if I meant to publish it.
What we believe will be read by many is scrutinised more closely than what is written for ourselves; what seemed true when conceived has often appeared false when I wrote it down.
If my writings have any value, those into whose hands they fall after my death can put them to whatever use they see fit.
Publishing the principles of my physics would provoke oppositions, controversies, and a reputation that would frequently divert me and rob me of the time set apart for my own improvement.
Our cares ought to extend beyond the present; it is good to forgo some profit to the living when we have in view ends of much greater advantage to posterity.
The little I have learned so far is almost nothing compared with what I am ignorant of and do not despair of attaining.
Discovering truth is like growing rich or winning battles: with sound principles great advances come easily, while admitting a false opinion on an important matter costs much more to recover from.
All my discoveries are consequences of five or six principal difficulties I have surmounted, and two or three similar victories would let me fully realise my designs.
I am not so far advanced in years that, in the ordinary course of nature, I may not still have leisure enough for this.
One is the more bound to husband the time that remains, the greater one's expectation of being able to employ it aright.
I am strongly bound to husband the time that remains to me.
My principles of physics are almost all so evident that understanding them suffices for assent, and I expect to demonstrate every one; yet they cannot agree with the diverse opinions of others.

meta.note: VI.6 restates it: my principles are 'of a kind the simplest and most evident'.

statements.text: Friends, indifferent parties, and envious critics have rarely objected anything I had not already considered, and no critic of my opinions has seemed more rigorous or equitable than myself.
The disputations of the schools have never brought to light any truth before unknown, since each side strives for victory by verisimilitude rather than weighing the reasons.
I cannot expect any profit from the objections that publishing my principles would provoke.

meta.note: Reply to the objection that opposition would reveal his errors, spread his views, and enlist helpers.

statements.text: I have not yet carried my thoughts far enough; much remains to be added before they can be applied to practice.
One cannot seize a thing and make it one's own so well when it has been learned from another as when one has discovered it oneself.
Acute persons who seemed to understand my opinions as I explained them have almost always, in repeating them, changed them so much that I could no longer acknowledge them as mine.

meta.note: He adds that the extravagances attributed to ancient philosophers whose writings are lost are likewise misrepresentations rather than their own absurdities.

statements.text: Scarcely in a single instance has a disciple of the ancient philosophers surpassed his master; the most devoted followers of Aristotle would be happy merely to know as much of nature as he did.
If anyone can carry my thoughts through to practice, it must be myself rather than another; this work cannot be finished so well by anyone but him who began it.
The advantage others would derive from the communication of my thoughts could not be very great.
Posterity should never believe on hearsay that anything has proceeded from me which I have not myself published.

The obscurity of the schools' distinctions and principles lets their users speak confidently of everything and defend anything without being convicted of error, like a blind man fighting in a dark cave.
Publishing my principles, which are the simplest and most evident, would be like letting daylight into that cave; such persons have an interest in my not publishing.
Those who wish to speak of all things and gain a reputation for learning succeed more easily by verisimilitude than by seeking truth, which unfolds slowly and only in some subjects.
Since I have examined everything in order, what remains to be discovered is harder than what I have found; anyone able to advance further than I could rediscover my findings for himself.
The habit acquired by seeking first what is easy and passing step by step to the harder will benefit an inquirer more than all my instructions.
Had I been taught in youth all the truths I have since demonstrated, I would probably never have known any beyond them nor acquired my facility in finding new ones.
Those who prefer knowledge of a few truths to the vanity of seeming ignorant of none need nothing more from me than this discourse in order to follow a course like mine.
Even superior minds have no reason for anxiety to learn the principles of my physics.
Those who volunteer their help from curiosity promise more than they perform, realise none of their fine designs, and expect repayment in explanations and compliments that waste one's time.
Besides his own hands, an inquirer can usefully employ only those of artisans he pays, whom the hope of gain stimulates to accuracy.

Experiments made by others are kept secret, or so laden with superfluous circumstances, and so ill described or even false because their makers saw in them only what agreed with their principles, that sorting them would not repay the time.
Even for a man known capable of the greatest discoveries, all that others could do would be to defray the expense of his experiments and protect his leisure from interruption.
I neither promise anything extraordinary, nor imagine the public much interested in my designs, nor have a soul so mean as to accept a favour I might be thought unworthy of.
Publishing my physics would not bring me any help with experiments that I could usefully accept.

meta.note: Not stated in so many words; it is the upshot of VI.7 and one of the considerations VI.8 says were taken together.

statements.text: I should publish this discourse together with some particular specimens of my philosophy, giving the public an account of my doings and designs.

meta.note: The specimens are the essays published with the Discourse (the Dioptrics and Meteorics are named in VI.10). This reconciles the case for communicating findings with withholding the physics.

statements.text: If I published nothing, many who knew of my earlier intention to publish might imagine my reasons for refraining were less to my credit than they really are.
I am not immoderately desirous of glory, and am even averse to it insofar as it is hostile to repose, which I value above everything else.

meta.note: A concession ('although I am not immoderately desirous of glory'). VI.12 adds that he will be more obliged to those who let him enjoy his retirement undisturbed than to any who offer the highest preferments; used in no inference.

statements.text: I have never sought to hide my actions as if they were crimes, since such concealment would wrong me and would disturb the tranquillity I seek.
Though indifferent alike to fame and to being forgotten, I have been unable to prevent myself from acquiring some sort of reputation.
I am bound to do my best at least to save myself from being ill spoken of.
My design of self-instruction suffers daily more delay for want of the countless experiments I need, which I cannot make without the assistance of others.
I owe it to myself not to give posterity ground to reproach me that things could have been left far more perfect had I made known how they might have helped.
I can select matters that provoke little controversy and expound no more of my principles than I wish, yet show clearly what I can and cannot accomplish in the sciences.
Readers who see an objection and my reply together will more easily determine where the truth lies.
Those who have objections to my writings should send them to my publisher, so that I may append my reply.

meta.note: He undertakes to avow errors frankly when convinced of them, or else briefly to state his defence, adding no new matter.

statements.text: In the Dioptrics and Meteorics the last matters are demonstrated by the first, which are their causes, and the first in turn by the last, which are their effects.
Experience renders the majority of these effects most certain.
The causes I deduce these effects from serve not to establish their reality but to explain their existence, while the reality of the causes is established by the reality of the effects.
My reasoning from causes to effects and from effects to causes is not the fallacy that logicians call a circle.
I call my starting points hypotheses only to signal that I believe I can deduce them from the first truths I have expounded, though I have expressly determined not to do so.
Some minds, thinking to master in a day what took another twenty years, would build extravagant philosophies on what they took to be my principles, and I would be blamed for it.
I should not, in these essays, deduce my hypotheses from my first principles.
If their reasons are well considered, my opinions will be found so simple and so conformed to common sense as to appear less extraordinary than any others on the same subjects.
I have adopted my opinions neither because others held them nor because they did not, but solely because reason has convinced me of their truth.

meta.note: Part VI's restatement of the first precept of method (II.7) as a description of his practice.

statements.text: Making and adjusting the machines I describe without overlooking the smallest detail requires skill and practice; success at the first attempt would be as astonishing as mastering the guitar in a day.
No one is entitled to condemn the invention explained in the Dioptrics because artisans cannot execute it at once.
Those who use their unprejudiced natural reason will be better judges of my opinions than those who heed only the writings of the ancients.
Those who unite good sense with study, whom alone I desire as judges, will not be so partial to Latin as to refuse my reasoning because it is in the vulgar tongue.
Writing in French reaches readers who use their natural reason but do not read Latin.

meta.note: Implicit: the choice of French only serves the stated purpose if the readers he wants as judges are reachable in French and not in Latin.

statements.text: I should write in French, the language of my country, rather than in Latin, the language of my teachers.
I should not bind myself to the public by any promise about my future progress that I am not certain of being able to fulfil.
My inclination is so opposed to all other pursuits, especially those that cannot help some without harming others, that I could not succeed in them if constrained to engage in them.

arguments.justification: Everyone is content with his share of good sense, and it is not likely that all are mistaken in this; so the conviction testifies that the power of judging rightly, which is what good sense means, is by nature equal in all.

Since reason is equal in all, unequal reason cannot explain why we disagree; and since what matters is applying the mind rightly, the difference must lie in the paths along which we conduct our thoughts and the objects we attend to.

The greatest minds fall into the greatest errors, and the slow traveller on the straight road outstrips the runner who leaves it; so capacity by itself secures nothing and right application is what counts.

Reason is what constitutes us as men, so it belongs to our form or nature; and difference of degree holds only among accidents, not among the forms of individuals of one species; hence reason is found complete in each individual.

meta.note: A second, independent argument for the same conclusion, adopted from 'the common opinion of philosophers'.

arguments.justification: The only qualities that perfect a mind are quickness of thought, imagination, memory and reason; in the first three I have wished to equal others, and reason is found complete in each individual; so in no respect is my mind more perfect than the common run.
The fruits I have already reaped from the method are such that I cannot help expecting the same of the future; what has increased my knowledge so far will go on increasing it.

Although, looking as a philosopher at the pursuits of mankind, I find scarcely one that is not vain and useless, the fruits I have already reaped from my method, and the expectation that it will go on augmenting my knowledge, give me such satisfaction that I believe that if any occupation of men as men is really excellent and important, it is the one I have chosen.

meta.note: The vanity of other pursuits is what the satisfaction overrides; it is kept as a premise because it gives the conclusion its conditional form ('if any occupation ...').

arguments.justification: The fruits I claim to have reaped from my method are these: truths of some importance discovered daily, of which other men are generally ignorant, and a satisfaction more perfect than any other I know; hence the highest satisfaction in the progress I believe I have made in the search for truth.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. The fruits announced in I.3 are described in III.5.

arguments.justification: Since we are so liable to deceive ourselves in what concerns us, my satisfaction with my own progress may itself be a delusion: copper and glass taken for gold and diamonds.

Because I may be deceived about myself and cannot trust the favourable judgments of friends, laying my course open for each reader to judge gives me, in the general opinion, a further aid to instruction that I would otherwise lack.

To give precepts is to claim greater skill than one's readers and to invite censure for the slightest error; I make no such claim for my mind, so I offer only a history of how I have conducted my own reason.

Precept-givers invite censure for the slightest error, but a tract put forth merely as a history or tale, offering examples to imitate and examples to avoid, claims no such authority; so I hope it will be useful to some and hurtful to none.

I studied where learned men must be found if they are found anywhere, was taught all that others learned there and read more besides, was judged no worse than fellows already marked out to teach, and lived in an age as rich in powerful minds as any; so my own case is a fair sample by which to judge all other men.

I was promised clear and certain knowledge from letters; yet the complete course of study left me with only doubts and the discovery of my ignorance. If I may judge others by myself, no one has found such a science, so it does not exist.

Each branch of the schools' studies has some genuine use or beauty, and even the most error-ridden repay some attention so that their worth can be judged; so, despite my disillusion, the studies as a whole still deserve esteem.

A narrative that admits impossible events, or that omits the mean and ordinary circumstances, does not represent life as it is; those who model their conduct on it therefore attempt projects beyond their powers, like the knights-errant of romance.

Reading the ancients is a kind of travel: a little of it corrects our judgment of our own customs, but too much makes us strangers to our own time. So the time I had already given them was sufficient.
Besides, fables and histories misrepresent life and lead those who take them as models into extravagant projects; so further time on them would not have served me.

meta.note: Second, independent reason ('Besides...').

arguments.justification: The best persuaders are those with the strongest reason, even without rhetoric, and the best poets those with the richest fancy, even without the art of poetry; so both excellences come from nature rather than from study.

Reasonings that are certain and evident make a foundation strong and solid; yet if all mathematics yields is the mechanical arts, nothing lofty has been raised on that foundation, which is what astonished me.

The ancients praise virtue magnificently but supply no criterion for it, so their fine names may cover apathy, pride, or worse; a magnificent structure with no secure foundation is a palace built on sand.

The revealed truths surpass our comprehension, and heaven is as open to the ignorant as to the learned; so my reason is neither competent to examine them nor needed for salvation, and examining them would require more than human help.
Every matter in philosophy is still disputed, and what the learned still dispute is not above doubt; therefore nothing in philosophy is above doubt.
The most distinguished minds have worked at philosophy for ages and settled nothing beyond doubt; my mind is no better than theirs; so I cannot expect to succeed where they have not.

Where learned men uphold many conflicting opinions on one matter and only one can be true, any particular opinion is far more likely false than true; so what is merely probable should be counted as well-nigh false.

The other sciences take their principles from philosophy, and nothing in philosophy is above doubt; since nothing solid can rest on uncertain foundations, no solid superstructure can be raised in them.

I had no need to sell science to make my fortune, and I cared little for honor obtained through fictitious titles; so neither the riches nor the honors the sciences promise could move me to cultivate them.

Having read even the most curious and rare books, and holding that some attention to every study is what lets us judge its worth and avoid deception, I had learned enough of the false sciences to see through their professors.

meta.note: Reconstructed link: Descartes states the premise (I.7) and the conclusion (I.13) but does not spell out the inference.

arguments.justification: For all these reasons together: letters yielded no certain science; I had read enough of the ancients; eloquence and poetry cannot be learned; mathematics, though certain, had nothing lofty built on it; the ancient morals rest on sand; theology is beyond reason; philosophy offers nothing beyond dispute and the merely probable is nearly false; the other sciences inherit philosophy's infirmity and their rewards do not tempt me; and the false sciences hold no more for me. Nothing remained to seek in books, so I turned to myself and to the world.

A man reasoning about his own affairs is soon punished by events if he judges badly, whereas a scholar's speculations carry no consequences and only reward vanity the further they stray from common sense; so the former holds far more truth.

Having resolved to seek knowledge only in myself or in the world, and wanting to learn to tell true from false, I should go where the truer reasoning is found: among men engaged in affairs that concern them, in courts and armies and every condition of life.

If great nations approve by common consent what seems absurd to us, and men's manners contradict one another as much as the philosophers do, then what our own custom approves may be equally absurd; persuasion by example and custom is therefore no ground for firm belief.
Having learned to withhold firm belief from whatever example and custom alone had persuaded me of, I gradually extricated myself from many errors.

Having given up books for either myself or the world, and having found in several years of studying the world no more settled conviction than in books, the remaining place to seek the truth I desired was myself; so I resolved to make myself my object of study and to use all my mind's powers in choosing my path.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. Descartes gives no explicit reason for the resolve; the elimination (letters, then the world, then myself) is the editor's reading of I.14-15.

arguments.justification: Because my years abroad had first rid me of many errors that darken the intelligence, the study of myself that followed succeeded better than it could have had I never left my country or my books.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. I.15 states the greater success without saying why; the connection through freed-from-many-errors is the editor's reading.

arguments.justification: Buildings and cities show the same pattern: what one hand plans freely comes out better than what many hands patch together over time. I take this to hold of works generally.

In the same way as with buildings and cities, laws determined piecemeal by many, under the pressure of particular crimes and disputes, will be less perfect than the appointments of a single wise legislator followed from the start.

The ordinances of the true religion are derived from God, a single legislator; so, as institutions that follow one wise legislator from the start are more perfect than those patched together by many, its constitution must be incomparably superior to that of every other.

meta.note: Veitch: 'It is thus quite certain'. The 'thus' is the translator's; in the original the sentence opens 'Comme il est bien certain que...' and offers the true religion as an evident parallel to the single-legislator case rather than as a consequence drawn from it. Recorded as an argument because the Veitch text, the file's source, phrases it as one.

arguments.justification: Sparta's laws taken singly were often strange and even opposed to good morals, so its pre-eminence cannot be due to their individual goodness. What remains is that they came from one man and all tended to a single end, which the principle says makes for perfection.

The book sciences without demonstrations are the opinions of many different individuals massed together, a work of many hands. By the principle they must be farther from truth than the simple inferences one man of good sense, using his natural and unprejudiced judgment, draws from his own experience.

Our judgments were formed under many conflicting authorities, our desires and our preceptors, rather than by reason alone. Like any work of many hands they cannot be as solid as if one mature reason had guided us from birth.

As no one pulls down all the houses of a town merely to rebuild it more handsomely, so a private individual should not overturn a state, or the body of the sciences and the order of teaching in the schools, which are large bodies of the same kind, in order to set it up amended.

Large bodies once overthrown are set up again only with great difficulty and their fall is always disastrous; and the defects of states, smoothed by custom, are almost always more tolerable than the change needed to remove them, as a well-worn mountain road is better followed than a straighter path over rocks and precipices. So a private individual should not overturn a state in order to set it up amended.

meta.note: A second, alternative support for the injunction alongside the town analogy; II.3's 'Hence it is' summarises the whole of II.2.

arguments.justification: Large bodies once overthrown are hard to set up again and their fall is disastrous; the defects of states have been smoothed by custom and are more tolerable than the change needed to remove them; whereas the difficulties in reforming my own opinions have remedies. So even the slightest public reform is incomparably harder than my private one.

A private individual may, and when the foundations are insecure must, take down his own house to rebuild it. My opinions are my own house; their foundations, principles taken on trust and judgments formed under desires and preceptors, are insecure; and, unlike public reform, the difficulties are remediable. So I should sweep them wholly away and rebuild, and will conduct my life far better than by leaning on old foundations.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. The I.13 principle (nothing-solid-on-uncertain-foundations) is added to make explicit why insecure foundations force rebuilding; II.2 relies on the house image alone. Descartes: 'I firmly believed that in this way I should much better succeed in the conduct of my life, than if I built only upon old foundations.'

arguments.justification: Hence: since it is preposterous for a private individual to set about reforming the state, those called by neither birth nor fortune to public affairs should not be forever projecting reforms of them.

The majority of men fall into two classes: the precipitate, who would lose their way for life if they once doubted their accustomed opinions, and the modest, who ought rather to follow their betters. For neither class is the design of stripping away all beliefs fitting, so it should not be undertaken by everyone.

Philosophers have defended every absurdity; nations opposed to us reason as well as we do; the same mind would think differently if raised elsewhere; fashions reverse within a decade. The best account of this variety is that our opinions rest on custom and example rather than on any certain knowledge.

I would have deferred, as the modest should, had I had one master or never seen how completely the learned disagree; but no opinion is so absurd that some philosopher has not held it, so there was no such master. Moreover our opinions rest on custom, which is no ground for firm belief; the majority is no guarantee of truth where truth is hard to find; and I could select no one whose opinions deserved preference. So there was no one to defer to, and I was constrained to use my own reason.

Having to rely on my own reason, and knowing that those who doubt hastily lose their way for life, I should go like a man walking alone in the dark: slowly and circumspectly, so that if I do not advance far I at least do not fall, and before dismissing any opinion first understand the task and find the true method.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. The II.3 premise (hasty-doubters-lose-their-way) is the editor's link: II.5 gives only the image of walking alone in the dark, which answers the danger II.3 describes.

arguments.justification: Logic, geometrical analysis, and algebra were the three arts I expected to contribute to my design. But logic serves to communicate rather than to discover, and its good precepts are buried among bad; analysis fatigues the imagination and algebra confuses the mind. By these considerations I was induced to seek another method with the advantages of the three and none of their defects.

As a state is best governed by a few laws rigidly administered rather than a multitude that hampers justice, so, in place of logic's many mixed precepts, a few precepts unfailingly observed would be perfectly sufficient for the method I seek.

Needing a method with the advantages of the three arts and none of their defects, and believing four precepts sufficient if never once neglected, I adopted these four, together with the firm resolution never to fail in observing them.

meta.note: The four precepts and the resolution are asserted jointly: Descartes presents them as one method, and the sufficiency claim is conditional on the resolution. The precepts are stipulated, not derived; this argument records their adoption in response to the need for a method. Their model is the geometers' practice of II.11 (geometers-reach-hard-conclusions-by-simple-chains), whose two provisos are the first and third precepts.

arguments.justification: The geometers reach their hardest conclusions by long chains of simple, easy reasonings. This led me to imagine that everything man can know is connected in the same way, and so is reachable provided we accept nothing false as true and always keep the order needed to deduce one truth from another.

I already knew one must begin with the simplest and easiest objects; and since, of all who have sought truth in the sciences, only the mathematicians have found demonstrations, I did not doubt that those objects are the ones they have examined.

Since one must begin with the simplest objects, and those are the objects the mathematicians examine, I resolved to begin there, expecting only to accustom my mind to truth and to a distaste for unsound reasoning.

I did not intend to master every particular science called mathematics; but since, however different their objects, they all consider only the proportions among them, it is best for my purpose to study proportions in the most general form, so that I can afterwards apply them to every class of objects where they legitimately hold.

To understand proportions I must sometimes consider them one by one and sometimes hold many in mind at once. Straight lines are the simplest and most distinctly imaginable objects for the former, and the briefest symbols are best for the latter.

Lines give the concreteness of geometrical analysis without confining the understanding to figures that fatigue the imagination; brief symbols give the compactness of algebra without its obscuring rules and formulas. So each of the two arts corrects the other's defects.

meta.note: The justification's account of which defect each device corrects is the editor's reading; Descartes says only that in this way he could borrow the best of both and correct the defects of each by the other.

arguments.justification: The reasonings of mathematics are certain and evident, whereas in philosophy, and in the sciences that borrow their principles from it, nothing is above doubt; so of all who have sought truth in the sciences, the mathematicians alone have found demonstrations, that is, certain and evident reasons.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. II.11 states the observation; I.10 and I.12 supply the contrast it rests on.

arguments.justification: Because I began with the simplest and most general truths, in the order the third precept prescribes, each truth I discovered was available as a rule for finding the ones that followed.

The accurate observance of these few precepts, beginning with the simplest and most general truths so that each truth found became a rule for the next, is what gave me such ease that in two or three months I solved questions I had thought very hard and determined how far others could be solved.

meta.note: Descartes reports the success as a fact and says the results are 'attributable to' starting with the simplest truths; the argument records that attribution.

arguments.justification: Since the truth on any point is one, whoever apprehends it has all that can be known on that point; a child who has correctly added by rule can be assured he has found everything human genius can find about that sum.

My third and fourth precepts teach adherence to the true order and an exact enumeration of all the conditions of the thing sought; that is all that gives certitude to the rules of arithmetic, so my method includes it.

meta.note: The child's arithmetic (whoever-grasps-truth-knows-all-on-that-point) is offered in II.12 to excuse his apparent vanity, not as a ground of this claim.

arguments.justification: Since I had not restricted the method to any particular matter, and it had succeeded so well in the two mathematical sciences, I hoped to apply it to the difficulties of the other sciences with no less success.

To attack all the difficulties of the sciences at once would violate the order the method prescribes; and knowledge of the sciences depends on principles borrowed from philosophy, in which I found nothing certain. So I must first try to establish the principles of philosophy.

Establishing the principles of philosophy is the most important inquiry and the one where precipitancy and anticipation in judgement are most to be dreaded; and I was only twenty-three. So I should not approach it until more mature, and should first prepare by eradicating my errors, gathering experience, and practising my method.

Just as one who pulls down the house he lives in must have another to live in while rebuilding, so I, having resolved to demolish my opinions and suspend judgement, still had to avoid irresolution in my actions and live as happily as I could; hence I needed a provisional morality to live by in the meantime.
Because action often cannot wait, suspending judgement must not become suspending action; I must not be irresolute in what I do.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.1 states the aim of not being irresolute without argument; III.3 supplies the reason.

arguments.justification: Having resolved to subject all my opinions to examination, I could not meanwhile rely on any of them; for the interim I held them for nought.
Since my own opinions are set aside and I must nevertheless act, I could not do better than follow, for the time being, the opinions of the most judicious.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.2 gives only the first premise; that action cannot wait is supplied from III.3 (see no-delay-forbids-irresolution), and III.1 states the same aim of not remaining irresolute.

arguments.justification: Even though people as judicious as ours may exist among the Persians and Chinese, expediency dictates that I regulate my practice by the opinions of those among whom I must live.
Since believing a thing and knowing that one believes it are different acts of mind, and the one is often found without the other, many people do not know what they really believe.

To learn the real opinions of the judicious I should look at what they do rather than what they say, for in the corruption of our manners few say exactly what they believe, so their words are an unreliable guide.
To learn the real opinions of the judicious I should look at what they do rather than what they say, for very many do not even know what they believe, so their words are an unreliable guide.

meta.note: Independent second reason for the same rule ('but also because ...').

arguments.justification: The most moderate opinions are always the most convenient for practice and probably the best, since all excess is generally vicious; so among opinions of equal repute I should choose the most moderate.
If I err, a moderate choice leaves me nearer the truth than an extreme would if the opposite extreme turned out to be right; so I should choose the moderate opinion.

meta.note: An independent second reason for the same rule.

arguments.justification: Because I find nothing on earth that is wholly beyond change, it would be a grave sin against good sense to bind myself to hold something good later merely because I approve of it now, when perhaps it will have ceased to be so.

Because I hope gradually to perfect my judgements rather than let them deteriorate, it would be a grave sin against good sense to bind myself to hold something good later merely because I approve of it now, when I may have ceased to esteem it such.

meta.note: Independent second reason for the same rule ('and because, for myself in particular ...'); III.2 pairs each reason with one clause of 'when perhaps it had ceased to be so, or I had ceased to esteem it such'.

arguments.justification: Since binding my future judgement is a sin against good sense, I place all promises that abridge freedom among the extremes that my rule of moderation tells me to avoid.

The truths of faith have always held first place in my belief and are above the reach of my reason; they are therefore not among the opinions I set aside for examination, and I adhere firmly to the faith I was raised in.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. Descartes reserves the truths of faith rather than arguing for them; the Part I statement (I.11) supplies the reason he gives elsewhere for not examining them.

arguments.justification: Obeying my country's laws and customs, keeping my faith, following the judicious people I live among, reading their real opinions in their practice, and preferring the most moderate of those opinions together make up my first maxim.
Since holding a steady course, even one chosen by chance, brings travellers at least to some place better than the middle of a forest, they ought to keep one direction rather than wander or stay put.

Since in action no delay is often permissible, when I cannot determine the truth I must act on the most probable; and where neither option is more probable I must still choose one rather than not act.

Since in action no delay is often permissible, the principle that when I cannot determine the truth I must act on the most probable, or else choose one course, is very certain; and that principle is the reason that determines my choice, so the reason is itself certain and true whatever opinion I choose.

Having chosen a course on the most probable opinion, or on an arbitrary one where nothing favours either, I should treat the choice as certain in practice, because the reason for making it, that I must act, is itself certain and true.
In holding to adopted opinions as steadfastly as if they were certain, I imitate travellers lost in a forest who keep going one way rather than wander or stand still.
If I must act on the most probable, choose one course even where none is more probable, and then treat the choice as certain in practice, then I should be as firm and resolute in my actions as I can.

meta.note: Independent of the travellers analogy; the principled derivation.

arguments.justification: Remorse comes from vacillating between courses for want of a determinate principle of choice; a firm resolve to hold the adopted course removes the vacillation and so the remorse.
If nothing but our thoughts is absolutely in our power, then once we have done our best in external things whatever we still fail in should be held, as regards us, impossible.

Since the will seeks only what the understanding presents as attainable, if we regard all external goods as equally beyond our power we will no more regret their absence than we regret not owning the kingdoms of China, or not having wings; we make a virtue of necessity.
If regarding external goods as beyond my power removes regret and desire for them, then this single persuasion suffices to keep me from desiring what I cannot obtain, and hence to make me content.

The ancient philosophers' happiness amid poverty is best explained by the prolonged discipline and incessant meditation on the limits nature set to their power that I confess maxim 3 requires: so convinced that only their thoughts were theirs, and the will seeking only what seems attainable, they ceased to desire other things and gained absolute command of their thoughts.
The philosophers who mastered their thoughts and desires in this way became happy; their example confirms that this persuasion suffices for contentment.

meta.note: Independent second support for the same conclusion.

arguments.justification: Those who command their thoughts can realise all their desires, whereas the favourites of fortune who lack this philosophy cannot; so the former have ground to think themselves richer, more powerful, freer and happier.

Since I should live as happily as I can, and accustoming myself to the persuasion that only my thoughts are in my power suffices for contentment, I should conquer myself rather than fortune and change my desires rather than the order of the world.

Reviewing the occupations of men, I could choose none better than the one I was already in, which I had long held to be the one truly excellent occupation of men as men: my method gives me the purest satisfaction I think possible in this life, and daily discoveries that leave me indifferent to everything else.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.5 gives the satisfaction and the discoveries as reasons; I.3 supplies the estimate of the occupation.

arguments.justification: Since God has given each of us a light of reason for distinguishing truth from error, I could not think it right to rest for a moment on another's opinions unless I meant to examine them by my own judgement as soon as I was able.

meta.note: III.5 argues from the light of reason alone; the II.4 resolve to use my own reason (must-use-own-reason) is the earlier resolution it echoes, not a premise.

arguments.justification: The first maxim is tolerable only if I mean to examine others' opinions myself; the second only if following doubtful opinions forfeits no better ones; the third only if I am on a sure path to knowledge and the true good. So all three rest on the design of continuing to instruct myself.
Since my whole provisional morality presupposes that I continue the work of instructing myself, continuing that work is the occupation I should keep.

meta.note: Offered as an additional reason ('Besides, the three preceding maxims were founded singly on the design of continuing the work of self-instruction').

arguments.justification: Since we seek or shun things only as the understanding judges them good or bad, right judgement is all that is needed for right action, and the most correct judgement for the best action.

The most correct judgement produces the best action, which is the acquisition of all the virtues and all else truly valuable within our reach; and assurance of acquiring these cannot fail to make us content.

Since right judgement suffices for right action and the most correct judgement for the best, that is for acquiring all the virtues and every other good within our reach, and assurance of that acquisition cannot fail to make us content, a path on which I am certain of attaining all the knowledge I am competent for is also the path to the largest amount of true good I can hope for; only on such a path could I restrain my desires and remain content.

The chief ground of my satisfaction with the method is the assurance of exercising my reason in all matters as well as I am able, and the habit of clearer and more distinct conceptions it forms in my mind; that is why, from the time I began to apply it, it has been a source of satisfaction so intense that I believe none more perfect or more innocent can be enjoyed in this life.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. II.13 gives the ground of the satisfaction that III.5 reports.

arguments.justification: Having resolved to sweep away my opinions, and now furnished with the provisional maxims that the rebuilding required, kept in reserve with the truths of faith, I may freely proceed to rid myself of the rest of my opinions.
Since there is more truth in men's reasonings about their own affairs than in a scholar's speculations, I hoped to examine my opinions better among men than shut up in my retreat.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.6 states the hope; I.14 gives the reason.

arguments.justification: Being free to examine my opinions, and hoping to do it better among people than in seclusion, I should resume travelling and examine them as a spectator of the world.
Set free to rid myself of my opinions, I made it my business in each matter to look for what could fairly be doubted and prove a source of error.
By reflecting in each matter on what might be doubted and prove a source of error, I gradually rooted out all the errors that had crept into my mind.
The sceptics doubt for the sake of doubting and seek nothing but uncertainty; my doubt sought assurance, rock beneath the sand; so my doubting everything was not imitating them.
Seeking assurance, and admitting as true only what I clearly know, I tested each opinion by clear and certain reasoning rather than by feeble conjecture.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.6 reports the practice of testing opinions by clear and certain reasoning; the first precept (II.7) is the rule it follows.

arguments.justification: When falsehood or uncertainty is established by clear and certain reasoning, even the most doubtful matter yields at least one certain conclusion, namely that it contains nothing certain.
As the ruins of a demolished house go into the new building, so in rooting out my ill-founded opinions I gathered observations and experience that I used in establishing more certain ones.

Travelling as a spectator, uprooting my errors, keeping their ruins as material and exercising my method throughout, I progressed further in truth than books or the company of scholars would have permitted, since reasoning about real affairs holds more truth than speculation.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.6 draws the conclusion from the nine years' activities; the I.14 principle that reasoning about real affairs holds more truth than speculation is the editor's gloss on why living among men outdid books.

arguments.justification: I had resolved never once to fail in observing my precepts, and to prepare for philosophy by continually exercising myself in my method; so throughout these years I continued to conduct my thoughts by its rules and set aside hours for mathematical problems and for questions of other sciences made almost mathematical.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.6 reports the practice; II.6 and II.13 are the resolutions it carries out.

arguments.justification: Since many men of the highest genius had attempted to found a more certain philosophy without success, the work must be one of very great difficulty.

I had resolved not to approach the principles of philosophy until I was more mature, and first to prepare by rooting out my errors, gathering experience and practising my method; so nine years passed without a determinate judgement on the disputes of the learned or a start on seeking firmer principles.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.7 reports the nine years without giving the reason; II.13 is the resolve they carry out. The difficulty of the inquiry (founding-a-certain-philosophy-is-very-difficult) is not why the nine years passed but why he might have waited longer still (rumour-brought-forward-the-inquiry).

arguments.justification: People credited me with a philosophy already completed; being unwilling to be thought other than I am, I had to make myself worthy of that reputation by every means.

The failure of the greatest minds made the inquiry look so difficult that I would not have begun it so soon; but the rumour that I had already completed it, and my wish to be worthy of that reputation, made me venture on it.

To make myself worthy of my reputation I need freedom from interruption; this country offers peace, solitude and the conveniences of a city all at once; so I should remove here, away from every place where my acquaintances could interrupt me.
Whether my foundations are secure can only be determined if I set them out; so, though these meditations may not be acceptable to everyone, I am in a measure constrained to advert to them.

meta.note: IV.1 concedes that the meditations may not be acceptable to everyone (first-meditations-may-not-be-acceptable-to-everyone); the concession is not a premise.

arguments.justification: In practice one must sometimes treat highly uncertain opinions as if beyond doubt, as my second maxim prescribes; but since I now wanted to attend solely to the search for truth, exactly the opposite procedure was called for. My first precept admits only what is beyond doubt, and I had long reckoned the merely probable as well-nigh false; so I resolved to reject as absolutely false everything in which I could imagine the least ground for doubt, in order to see whether anything wholly indubitable remained in my belief.

meta.note: Reconstructed link (cross-part premises). IV.1 grounds the rejection of the doubtful only in the aim of attending solely to the search for truth; the first precept (II.7) and the Part I rule to reckon the merely probable as well-nigh false (I.12) are supplied as the standards it applies in strict form. IV.1 recalls the second maxim of Part III (maxim-2-be-firm-and-resolute) only to set it aside: what practice requires is exactly inverted in the search for truth. The maxim is the contrast, not a ground of the doubt.

arguments.justification: Since the senses sometimes deceive us, whatever they present admits of doubt, and my resolve requires me to suppose that nothing exists as they present it.

Some men fall into paralogisms even on the simplest matters of geometry, and I am as liable to error as anyone; so every reasoning I had taken for a demonstration admits of doubt and, by my resolve, must be rejected as false.

The very same thoughts we have awake can occur in sleep, when none of them is true; so nothing distinguishes my waking presentations from the illusions of dreams, and by my resolve I suppose they have no more truth.

Having resolved to reject as false whatever admits the least ground for doubt, and having accordingly supposed that nothing is as the senses present it, that my former demonstrations are false and that my waking thoughts are no truer than dreams, I am in the state of doubting everything: I doubt.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.1 draws the cogito from 'whilst I thus wished to think that all was false'; that wish is the doubt the method of doubt produces, so the doubt is not a bare starting point.

arguments.justification: From the very circumstance that I thought to doubt of the truth of other things, it is evident that I am thinking; doubting is itself a mode of thought.
While I wished to think that everything was false, it was absolutely necessary that I, who was thinking this, should be something; in order to think one must exist; therefore I exist.

Even under the most extravagant suppositions, that the senses present nothing real, that my former demonstrations are false, that my waking thoughts are no truer than dreams, the supposing is itself thinking and thinking requires existing; so no ground of doubt the sceptics can allege is capable of shaking this truth.

meta.note: The three doubt-suppositions are consumed here as the test the cogito passes.

arguments.justification: I had resolved to accept only what is wholly indubitable; 'I think, therefore I am' is the one truth that no doubt can shake; so I may without scruple take it as the first principle of the philosophy I seek.

meta.note: Reconstructed link (cross-part premises). The first precept (II.7) is the positive rule under which the surviving truth is accepted; IV.1 states only the resolve and the acceptance.

arguments.justification: The principles of philosophy had to be established before anything else, and my doubting had never sought anything but ground for assurance; so in these first meditations I gave my attention solely to the search for truth, to find whether anything in my belief was wholly indubitable.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.1 states the aim; II.13 (the principles of philosophy come first) and III.6 (my doubt seeks assurance) supply the resolutions it carries out. That the provisional code left him free to doubt (III.6) and that the rumour made him begin when he did (III.7) are the occasion of the first meditations, not grounds of their aim, and are not premises.

arguments.justification: I have never thought my mind more perfect than the common run, and other men fall into paralogisms even on the simplest matters of geometry; so I am as open to error as any of them.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.1 says 'convinced that I was as open to error as any other'; I.2 is where that modest estimate of his own mind is stated.

arguments.justification: I can suppose I have no body and that there is no world or place in which I am, yet I cannot suppose that I am not; from my doubting it follows that I am; whereas had I merely ceased to think I would have had no reason to believe I existed even if everything else were real. So thinking alone is my essence, and my existence needs no place and depends on no material thing.

Since my whole nature is to think, and that nature needs no place and depends on nothing material, the 'I', the mind by which I am what I am, is wholly distinct from the body, is even more easily known than the body, and would remain all that it is even if the body did not exist.

Having found one proposition I know to be true, I sought what makes it certain; in 'I think, therefore I am' nothing assures me of its truth except that I see very clearly that to think one must exist. So I may take as a general rule that whatever we conceive very clearly and distinctly is true.
I doubt, and it is a greater perfection to know than to doubt; so my being is not wholly perfect.

I asked whence I had learned to think of something more perfect than myself. My ideas of the sky, the earth, light, heat and the like contain nothing superior to me, so they could come from my own nature, or from its imperfection if they are false; but this could not be the case with the idea of a nature more perfect than mine. I could not have received it from nothing, which is manifestly impossible; nor from myself, since it is no less repugnant that the more perfect should be an effect of the less perfect than that something should come from nothing. It remained that it was placed in me by a nature really more perfect than mine, possessing every perfection of which I can form an idea; in a word, God.

meta.note: IV.4 contrasts this with the ideas of sky, earth, light and heat, which need no source beyond myself (ideas-of-lesser-things-explicable-by-my-nature); the contrast is not a premise.

arguments.justification: Having the idea of a being more perfect than myself while my own being is not wholly perfect, I know of perfections that I do not possess.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.4 asserts that I know perfections I do not possess without deriving it; the derivation from the idea of a more perfect being and my own imperfection is the editor's.

arguments.justification: Since I know perfections I do not possess, I am not the only being. Had I existed alone and independently, having from myself the little perfection I possess, I could for the same reason have given myself all the perfection I lack and become infinite, eternal, immutable, omniscient and all-powerful. I have not; so there is necessarily some other, more perfect Being on whom I depend and from whom I have received all that I possess.

meta.note: Second, independent argument for God's existence. IV.4 concludes to 'some other more perfect Being'; the identification with the wholly perfect God is asserted in the following sentence ('whose existence has been established by the preceding reasonings'), not argued.

arguments.justification: To know the nature of God, whose existence the preceding reasonings established, as far as my own nature permits, I had only to consider, for every property of which I find some idea in my mind, whether possessing it is a mark of perfection; and I was assured that none which indicates imperfection is in him and that none of the rest is lacking.

meta.note: IV.4 proceeds from God's existence as the all-perfect being alone; that my idea of perfection comes from him (my-idea-of-perfection-comes-from-god) is not used.

arguments.justification: Whatever I would gladly be rid of is a mark of imperfection; I would be happy to be free of doubt, inconstancy and sadness, so they mark imperfection; and no imperfection is in God.

I could not deny that the ideas of sensible and corporeal things were really in my thoughts, which raised the question whether God might be corporeal as well as intelligent. But I had already clearly recognised that the intelligent nature is distinct from the corporeal; all composition is evidence of dependency, and dependency is manifestly imperfection; so it could not be a perfection in God to be compounded of these two natures, and consequently he is not so compounded.

meta.note: The question is raised by the ideas of corporeal things being really in my thought (ideas-of-corporeal-things-really-in-my-thought); that occasion is not a premise.

arguments.justification: Whatever is not wholly perfect is dependent, as I found in my own case, and that on which it depends is the wholly perfect Being; so if there are bodies, intelligences or other natures that are not wholly perfect, their existence depends on God's power such that they could not subsist without him for a single moment.

meta.note: Descartes gives this with a bare 'but that'; the step uses the converse of the stated axiom dependency-is-imperfection, surfaced as imperfection-implies-dependency.

arguments.justification: Going over some of the geometers' simplest demonstrations, I observed that the great certainty accorded to them by common consent rests solely on their being clearly conceived in accordance with the rule I had laid down.

meta.note: IV.5 sets the scene with the geometers' object (geometers-object-is-extended-space); the certainty claim rests on clear conception alone.

arguments.justification: Nothing in a geometrical demonstration assures me that its object exists: I perceive that a triangle's angles equal two right angles without perceiving that any triangle exists. But returning to the idea of a Perfect Being, I found that existence is comprised in it just as that equality is comprised in the idea of a triangle, or the equidistance of all points from the centre in the idea of a sphere, or even more clearly; and since geometrical demonstrations are certain because clearly conceived, it is at least as certain that God, this Perfect Being, exists as any demonstration of geometry can be.

meta.note: Third argument for God's existence. Together with divine-guarantee this closes the Cartesian circle: the criterion supports God's existence and God's existence supports the criterion. IV.5 sets the disanalogy with geometry (geometry-does-not-prove-existence-of-its-objects) as a contrast, not a premise.

arguments.justification: Those who never raise their thoughts above sensible objects consider everything by way of imagination, a mode of thinking limited to material things; but God and the soul are not material and their ideas were never in the senses; so to such people what cannot be imagined seems unintelligible, as if one tried to hear sounds or smell odours with one's eyes.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.6 states the diagnosis and then offers the schools' maxim as evidence for it (schools-maxim-shows-reliance-on-imagination); deriving it from the immateriality of the mind (IV.2) is the editor's reading.

arguments.justification: That even the philosophers of the schools accept as a maxim that nothing is in the understanding which was not first in the senses, when the ideas of God and of the soul have certainly never been there, makes it manifest how far men consider nothing except by way of imagination and the senses, so that what cannot be imagined seems to them unintelligible.

The schools hold that there is nothing in the understanding which was not previously in the senses; but the idea of God, like that of the soul, is in my understanding and has certainly never been in the senses; so the maxim is false.

The certainty of geometry rests solely on its demonstrations being clearly conceived, and that rule is itself certain only because God exists, is a Perfect Being, and is the source of all we possess; and no reason can remove the doubt cast on any other knowledge unless it presupposes God; so the certainty of geometry, and of everything else we take ourselves to know, depends on God.

We have a moral assurance that we have a body and that stars and an earth exist, so strong that doubting them seems extravagant; yet when asleep we can imagine ourselves with another body and seeing other stars and another earth when there is nothing of the kind, and dream thoughts are often no less vivid and distinct than waking ones. So no one of sound mind can deny that, for metaphysical certainty, entire assurance about these things is excluded, whereas the existence of the soul and of God has been established by reasons that survive this doubt.

Our ideas or notions, to the extent of their clearness and distinctness, are real and proceed from God, since all that we possess is derived from him; and it is no less repugnant that falsity should proceed from God than that truth should proceed from nothing; so to that extent they must be true.

meta.note: Second justification of the criterion of truth; with criterion-from-cogito and ontological-argument it forms a cycle (the Cartesian circle), which the format records as a strongly connected component.

arguments.justification: What is clear and distinct in our ideas is real, proceeds from God and is true; falsity cannot proceed from God; so any falsity our ideas contain can only lie in what is confused and obscure, which in that respect proceeds from nothing, and is in us because we are not wholly perfect.

Because I am not wholly perfect, some of my ideas may be false; the only thing that assures me that those which are clear and distinct are true is that what is real in them proceeds from a Perfect and Infinite Being, from whom no falsity can come. So the rule is certain only because God exists, is perfect, and is the source of all we possess; had we not known this, however clear and distinct our ideas, we should have no ground for assurance of their truth.

However long men of the highest genius study the question, any reason for holding waking thoughts true rather than dreams must rest on the rule that what we clearly and distinctly conceive is true; and that rule is certain only through God; so no reason can remove the doubt unless it presupposes God's existence.

The rule attaches truth to the clearness and distinctness of an idea, not to the state in which it occurs; so if a geometer discovered a new demonstration while asleep, his being asleep would not militate against its truth.

The most ordinary error of dreams is to represent objects as our external senses do; but we are deceived in the same way when awake, as when the jaundiced see everything yellow or distant bodies look smaller than they are; so this error is not prejudicial and rightly leads us to suspect the ideas of sense.

After the knowledge of God and of the soul has made the rule certain, the truth of waking thoughts need not be questioned because of dreams: a very distinct idea would be true even if it came in sleep, and the ordinary error of dreams merely reproduces the errors of sense, which we suffer awake as well; neither touches what reason clearly conceives.

Neither the senses nor the imagination can assure us of anything unless the understanding intervenes; only what reason clearly conceives is true. So whether awake or asleep we ought never to be persuaded of the truth of anything except on the evidence of our reason.

meta.note: IV.8 illustrates the rule with the sun's apparent size and the imagined chimaera (senses-and-imagination-do-not-establish-existence); the illustration is not a premise.

arguments.justification: Reason plainly tells us that all our ideas or notions contain some truth; for otherwise it could not be that God, who is wholly perfect and veracious, should have placed them in us.

Because of our partial imperfection not all our thoughts can be true; truth is to be judged by reason, not by the liveliness of imagination; and our reasonings are never so clear or complete in sleep as when awake; so reason dictates that the thoughts possessing truth are to be found in waking experience rather than in dreams.

Holding firmly to the single principle by which I demonstrated the existence of God and of the soul, and admitting nothing that did not appear more clear and certain than the demonstrations of the geometers once had, I found means in a short time to satisfy myself on all the principal difficulties usually treated in philosophy.

God established these laws and impressed such notions of them on our minds that, after sufficient reflection, we cannot doubt them; and what is conceived so clearly and distinctly is true; therefore the laws are exactly observed in all that exists or takes place in the world.

Exhibiting the whole chain of truths would require treating many questions in dispute among the learned, with whom I do not wish to be embroiled; so it is better to mention only in general what these truths are.
With no other principle on which to found my reasonings than the infinite perfection of God, I demonstrated all the laws of nature about which there could be any room for doubt.
Because the laws are demonstrated from the infinite perfection of God alone, and that perfection is the same whatever he creates, no world he might create could fail to observe them.

By describing only what would happen in a new world I can throw the disputed subjects into the shade and express my judgement with greater freedom, without being obliged to adopt or refute the opinions of the learned.

Since purely material things could really have come to their present state from chaos by the laws alone, and their nature is far easier to conceive when they are seen coming gradually into existence, describing them in this way is the more intelligible course.

meta.note: An independent second reason for the same decision; kept as a separate argument.

arguments.justification: Given matter with only the properties everyone naturally understands, agitated into chaos and left to God's ordinary concurrence, the laws of nature, which no world God created could fail to observe, require the greater part of it to dispose itself as heavens, while some parts compose an earth, some planets and comets, and others a sun and fixed stars.

From the nature of the matter that composes the sun and the stars under these laws, I expounded what the light found in them must be, how it traverses the immense spaces of the heavens in an instant, and how it is reflected from the planets and comets toward the earth.

Having described the substance, situation, motions and qualities of these heavens and stars and the nature and propagation of their light, I had said enough to show that nothing observable in the heavens or stars of our system must not, or at least may not, appear precisely alike in the world described.

Following the same laws, the parts of the earth so formed must tend toward its centre even though God gave its matter no weight; with water and air on its surface the heavens and especially the moon must cause an ebb and flow like our tides and an east-to-west current like that between the tropics; and mountains, seas, springs, rivers, metals, plants and all mixed bodies might be formed in it naturally.

Since besides the stars nothing I know of produces light except fire, I set out from the same laws all that pertains to its nature, production and support, and showed how it yields heat without light or light without heat, induces colours and other qualities, liquefies some bodies and hardens others, consumes almost all to ashes and smoke, and from ashes by its mere intensity forms glass.

Since the action by which God now sustains the world is the very action by which he created it, his having established the laws of nature and lent his concurrence to a mere chaos would suffice, in the course of time, to bring purely material things to the state we now observe; so this can be believed without discredit to the miracle of creation.

Whatever is not wholly perfect depends on God's power so completely that it could not subsist without him for a single moment; so the action by which he sustains the world from moment to moment is nothing other than the action by which he created it.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. V.2 cites the doctrine as commonly received among theologians; IV.4 supplies the metaphysical ground Descartes himself established for it.

arguments.justification: When I examined what functions could exist in such a body as consequences of this supposition, I found precisely all those that exist in us independently of any power of thinking, but none of those that depend on thought alone and belong to us as men.
The soul is the part of us distinct from the body, whose whole nature consists in thinking; so the functions that exist in us independently of any power of thinking owe nothing at all to it.

The distinctively human functions were absent from the body alone and appeared as soon as a rational soul was supposed created and joined to it in a particular manner; so a real man is such a body united with a rational soul.

To show how I handled the animal body in the treatise, I give the explanation of the motion of the heart and arteries, because as the first and most general motion observed in animals it affords the means of readily determining what to think of all the rest.

Just as any liquid allowed to fall drop by drop into a highly heated vessel at once expands and dilates, so the heat of the heart, greater than anywhere else in the body, makes each drop of blood that enters its cavities rapidly expand and dilate.

The hollow vein and venous artery are always full and their orifices toward the heart cannot be closed while its cavities are empty, so blood necessarily flows in; being at once rarefied by the heat, the two large drops expand the whole heart, press shut the five inlet valves so no more blood comes down, and push open the six outlet valves, swelling the arterial vein and great artery; as the blood cools, the heart and arteries contract, the six valves close, the five reopen, and two more drops enter to begin again.

The motion I have explained follows from the arrangement of the parts that may be seen in the heart by the eye alone, from the heat that may be felt with the fingers, and from the nature of the blood as learned from experience, just as the motion of a clock follows from the power, situation and shape of its counterweights and wheels.

meta.note: Aimed at those who cannot distinguish true reasons from mere verisimilitudes.

arguments.justification: A moderate ligature hinders the blood already in the arm from returning toward the heart by the veins but cannot stop new blood coming forward through the arteries, which lie deeper, have firmer coats that are harder to compress, and carry blood from the heart with more force than the veins return it; since that blood escapes through the opened vein, there must be passages below the ligature through which it reaches the veins from the arteries.

The heart sends blood out into the arteries and never receives it back by that route, the arteries pass it through the small passages at their extremities into the small branches of the veins, and the veins return it to the heart; so its course amounts precisely to a perpetual circulation.

meta.note: Harvey's discovery, which Descartes accepts. Only the one-way passage of blood out of the heart is needed here, not Descartes' own rarefaction account of why the heart beats.

arguments.justification: The valves along the veins permit blood only to return from the extremities to the heart, never to pass outward from the middle of the body; so the blood in the veins must have reached the extremities by another route, the arteries, and be on its way back to the heart.

meta.note: Second, independent support attributed to Harvey.

arguments.justification: If all the blood in the body can leave in a short time through one cut artery, even one tied close to the heart and cut between the heart and the tie so that it can only have come from the heart, then all the blood in the body passes through the heart and out by the arteries.

meta.note: Third, independent support attributed to Harvey.

arguments.justification: Because the blood that leaves the heart by the arteries returns to it by the veins, the veins are never emptied by feeding the heart nor the arteries overfilled by receiving all the blood that passes through it.

The difference between the blood of the veins and that of the arteries can only arise from its being rarefied and, as it were, distilled by passing through the heart, which is why it is thinner, livelier and warmer just after leaving the heart and why the difference is marked only in the neighbourhood of the heart.

The consistency of the coats of the arterial vein and the great artery shows that the blood is impelled against them with more force than against the veins, as it would be if it were driven out of the heart by rarefaction.

Why should the left cavity and the great artery be wider than the right cavity and the arterial vein, unless the blood of the venous artery, having already passed through the heart and been in the lungs, is thinner and rarefies more readily and to a higher degree than the blood coming straight from the hollow vein?

meta.note: Descartes also cites the pulse: physicians could infer nothing from it unless blood of differing nature were rarefied to differing degrees by the heart's warmth.

arguments.justification: The blood is heated anew each time it passes through the heart and is then carried to every part of the body; that is why withdrawing blood from a part withdraws its heat, and why a heart as hot as glowing iron could not warm the hands and feet unless it continually sent them new blood.

meta.note: Offered in V.7 as a further circumstance evincing that rarefaction is the true cause of the motion of the blood; recorded here in the explanatory direction.

arguments.justification: The blood rarefied almost into vapour in the right ventricle passes to the lungs, where the fresh air brought in by breathing thickens it and converts it anew into blood before it enters the left cavity; without this it would be unfit to nourish the fire there.

meta.note: Offered in V.7 as a further circumstance evincing that rarefaction is the true cause of the motion of the blood; recorded here in the explanatory direction.

arguments.justification: Animals without lungs have only one cavity in the heart, and unborn children, who cannot use their lungs, have a hole and a tube by which the blood bypasses them; this is just what should be expected if the office of the lungs were to re-thicken blood rarefied in the right ventricle.

The heart sends heat and the more fluid parts of the blood to the stomach through the arteries to dissolve the food; the juice of food becomes blood by being distilled through the heart perhaps one or two hundred times a day; and the force with which the rarefied blood passes toward the extremities leaves some of its parts in the members, selected by the situation, shape and smallness of the pores they meet, as variously perforated sieves separate different kinds of grain.

meta.note: Offered in V.7 as a further circumstance evincing that rarefaction is the true cause of the motion of the blood; recorded here in the explanatory direction.

arguments.justification: The most agitated and penetrating parts of the blood are the fittest to compose the animal spirits, and they reach the brain simply because the arteries that carry them leave the heart in the most direct lines and, by the rules of mechanics which are those of nature, when many parts tend at once to a point without room for all, the stronger drive the weaker aside; from the brain the spirits pass through the nerves into the muscles and give motion to all the members.

meta.note: Offered in V.7 as a further circumstance evincing that rarefaction is the true cause of the motion of the blood; recorded here in the explanatory direction.

arguments.justification: Given the fabric of the nerves and muscles and the spirits that move them, changes in the brain suffice to produce waking, sleep and dreams, the ideas impressed by light, sound, odour, taste and heat and by hunger and thirst, the common sense that receives them, the memory that retains them, the fantasy that recombines them and distributes the spirits to the muscles, and movements as suited to objects as ours are apart from the will; as we see heads still move and bite the earth shortly after being struck off, though no longer animated.
